subsubtopic: CONDEMNATION OF PRIME MINISTER'S ATTITUDE TOWARDS UNEMPLOYED IN NEWFOUNDLAND-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. I do so out of a sense of indignation. Mr. Speaker, we in this House have come to accept the arrogance of the Prime Minister in dealing with the economic problems facing this country today, but I do not think any of us, and especially the rest of the country, was quite prepared for the Prime Minister's performance in St. John's yesterday when confronted with an orderly and peaceful demonstration of the unemployed. As a Canadian, and not just as a Newfoundlander, I do not and cannot accept the Prime Minister's "Rich Man-Poor Man" concept of confederation, which would have the poorer provinces content with acceptance of the crumbs from the table of the richer provinces. I would move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Humbert St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall):
That in the opinion of this House, the Prime Minister should try living in Newfoundland, the province with the highest per capita cost of living in the country, for a period of one month on $115 per week, which amount is the maximum payable under Canada Works, and should then be directed to report to this House on the adequacy of the government's make-work programs.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-REASON FOR GIVING AID TO FOREIGN STATES IN VIEW OF SITUATION IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, I should like to put my first question to the Minister of Finance who is the chief spokesman for the government on economic affairs in this country. My

question arises out of the views expressed by the Prime Minister in St. John's, Newfoundland yesterday to the effect that the principle of Confederation is that there are some rich and some poor, and in effect, if they do not like it down there, that is just too bad.
Is the minister aware that tens of millions of dollars are being poured by the federal Export Development Corporation into the states of Texas, New Jersey and Minnesota to aid the construction of steel mills in those states, notwithstanding that the unemployment there is as low as 3.5 per cent and the average unemployment is one-third of that in Newfoundland? If he is aware of that type of financing going into the United States, would he indicate why it is the government's policy to help the citizens of Texas, and those other states, more than the citizens of Newfoundland who are crying for jobs?

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-REASON FOR GIVING AID TO FOREIGN STATES IN VIEW OF SITUATION IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-REASON FOR GIVING AID TO FOREIGN STATES IN VIEW OF SITUATION IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is asking a very, very mixed type of question. What the Prime Minister said is something that everyone in Canada pretty well understands. Unfortunately, all provinces of Canada are not equally rich in natural resources. In terms of history, some provinces become rich and then poor. It is the federal government's role to attempt to equalize opportunities in Canada, and that is why we have equalization programs and work programs for the less fortunate Canadians to benefit in Confederation.
With regard to the second part of the question, I do not know exactly to what the hon. member is referring. I will look into that and provide him with a reply.

U117) UNEMPLOYMENT-POSSIBILITY OF AID TO REFURBISH FISHING FLEET IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, again to the Minister of Finance. In view of the fact that EDC has agreed to put out something over $100 million in the form of long term loans at low interest rates to Great Britain and various states in the United States for the construction of steel mills; in view of the fact that over $160 million has been lent to Poland to help build a pulp and paper mill in that country, and other money has gone to Iran; would the minister at least undertake to review this situation to see if this money could be used, for example, to help refurbish fishing fleets off the Atlantic coast and in that way give a few more jobs to Canadians?

subtopic: U117) UNEMPLOYMENT-POSSIBILITY OF AID TO REFURBISH FISHING FLEET IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
The hon. member's question puzzles me because we have an organisation that helps to export Canadian technology and Canadian materials abroad in order to create jobs in Canada, but members opposite are not happy with that. I am completely puzzled. If the hon. member is putting the proposition that we should not try to get into international markets and should have a completely closed internal economy, and if he thinks that is going
November 25, 1977

to build prosperity in Canada, I hope Canadians will never accept such a policy with such a person to lead it.

subtopic: U117) UNEMPLOYMENT-POSSIBILITY OF AID TO REFURBISH FISHING FLEET IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext: I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. Would the minister indicate whether the government has considered not only exporting the technology that we are talking about to help others in the world, but using that technology to help people such as those who are out of work in Newfoundland? You could do two things. You could create more work for those who have the technology, and secondly you could create the work right here in Canada within that area where you have 17.5 per cent unemployment, compared to 3.5 per cent unemployment in Minnesota.

subtopic: U117) UNEMPLOYMENT-POSSIBILITY OF AID TO REFURBISH FISHING FLEET IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am really surprised by the comments of the hon. member. In a modern society, should I explain to him, when we have reached a degree of sophistication which allows us to sell our technology it is normal to do so. I would like to tell him that if we do not sell Canadian machinery or technical services in Poland for the construction of a paper mill, if we did not sell those products and that technology, some other countries would willingly do so. In the competitive world in which we are living it is absolutely normal to sell abroad the products used to develop those industries. It is normal and it shows the degree of competitiveness that Canada has reached in fields in which we are specialized. I do not understand the hon. member who does not want us to use our assets to create jobs for Canadian workers manufacturing equipment, for Canadian engineers who can show abroad that Canadians have made great progress in the past few years.

REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF DEPUTY MINISTER'S STATEMENT ON TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I should like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister if he could indicate whether the statement made yesterday by the deputy minister of industry, trade and commerce is government policy? Regarding the negotiations on tariff concessions, he said that there are going to be some winners and most assuredly some losers. Because of the concern that will be aroused by this kind of general statement can the Deputy Prime Minister tell the House who the winners are, who the losers are and whether this is an accurate reflection of government policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF DEPUTY MINISTER'S STATEMENT ON TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may return to the original question I can tell the hon. member that it is the intention of the Minister of Finance to make an announcement on the footwear decision next week. Regarding the comments of the deputy minister of industry, trade and commerce, may I say that at the present time the Canadian government is preparing its negotiating stance. In fact, the major participants in the negotiations have not fully agreed upon a tariff plan that will be the subject of negotiations. It is obvious, however, that if any adjustments are to be made in the Canadian tariff it is the intention of the government to ensure that reciprocal benefits accrue to the Canadian economy. The objective is that the over-all wealth of the trading community be increased and accordingly the over-all prospects of Canada in the fields of employment and income will be improved as a result of the negotiations. We are looking at the negotiations as an opportunity to increase trade for Canada with a resultant increase in our over-all prosperity. I think in a narrow sense it may be possible to look at the situation in terms of particular industries that have tariff reductions, but over-all we hope it means growth in the prosperity of the country.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER RECENT AGREEMENT ON PENSIONS WITH ITALY APPLIES TO QUEBEC
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Could the minister advise the House whether the general agreement which the federal government signed recently with the Prime Minister of Italy applies to all Canadians, including those Quebecers who are entitled to Canadian pension plan benefits, or whether they are excluded from this agreement, Quebec not having signed this agreement with Italy as yet?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER RECENT AGREEMENT ON PENSIONS WITH ITALY APPLIES TO QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I indicated yesterday how I deplore the statement by the Quebec premier that there had been no consultations between Quebec and Ottawa concerning the agreement signed by Canada and Italy. Yesterday, my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs tabled in the House the correspondence on this subject which clearly bears witness to the fact that the federal government has vainly tried over the past ten months to involve the Quebec government in these negotiations. I can assure the hon. member that the Canada-Italy agreement provides all Canadian citizens, including those residing in Quebec, with the relevant benefits of the old age security pension scheme, the family allowances plan, and of course the Canada Pension Plan for those Quebec residents who are covered by it; as the hon. member knows perfectly well, however, most Quebec residents are covered by the Quebec Pension Plan, not the Canada Pension Plan, and this situation will have to be dealt with under a special agreement between the Quebec Pension Board and its Italian counterpart, under the general agreement which Canada signed with Italy during Prime Minister Andreotti's visit to Ottawa. subsubtopic: REASON FOR ALLEGED EXPANSION OF DEPARTMENT'S MANDATE WITHOUT APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
What is being done essentially, Mr. Speaker, is that the Canadian government has entrusted the Department of Urban Affairs with analyzing, developing and coordinating policies on urban matters while the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is responsible for housing assistance. So we have tried to integrate those two government sectors into a more rational structure to improve efficiency and eliminate duplication.

Therefore some of the laid off employees have criticized and made statements to the press which exaggerate the scope of these changes. Since the hon. member comes from the private sector, I am sure she knows very well that to improve efficiency one must undertake some adjustments to be more efficient and save money to the Canadian taxpayers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Labour. speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT VIEW OF STATISTICS RELEASED BY INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the statistics revealed by the International Labour Organization are entirely erroneous as far as Canada is concerned. For one thing, the basis of comparison is faulty. subtopic: GOVERNMENT VIEW OF STATISTICS RELEASED BY INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANIZATION

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On December 22, 1976 the minister announced in the House the policy of the government with respect to strengthening the safeguards requirements which apply to the export of
Oral Questions
Canadian reactors and uranium. May I just quote the relevant sentence in what he said, Mr. Speaker. He said: "Shipments to non-nuclear weapon states under future contracts will be restricted to those which satisfy the non-proliferation treaty or otherwise accept international safeguards on their entire nuclear program."
Last night in Brussels the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said that Canada is becoming less and less able to restrict the sales of its nuclear technology, and went on to give as a reason the possible commercial retaliation by West Germany. In view of this shocking departure from government policy by a minister who is reported to have made this statement with a laugh, will the Secretary of State for External Affairs now reaffirm his statement of last December and repudiate the statement of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SAFEGUARDS APPLICABLE TO EXPORT OF NUCLEAR REACTORS AND URANIUM-REQUEST FOR RESTATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I read the newspaper report, but I have not, of course, discussed this with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. From what I was able to deduce from it, he was in fact outlining what is a very serious problem, and I think all hon. members are aware of it, namely that it is getting to be extremely difficult to get international agreement on the whole question of nuclear controls. But that having been said, I am very happy to tell the hon. member that there has been no change in terms of the basic policy of the government. We are still of the view that we ought not to deal in nuclear supplies or technology with countries which do not sign the non-proliferation treaty or accept full scope safeguards.

Income Tax Act

The House resumed from Thursday, November 24, consideration in committee of Bill C-l 1, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to provide other authority for the raising of funds-Mr. Chretien-Mr. Laniel in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. When the House adjourned last night, the committee was considering clause 1.
On clause 1.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to clause 1, certain of my colleagues will deal with general matters but I should like to deal with some quite specific aspects of the clause. As the explanatory notes indicate, "This amendment, which substitutes the underlined amount for $1,000, would implement paragraph (1) of the ways and means motion to amend the Income Tax Act", so that the amount an individual may claim against capital gains will be increased from $1,000 to $2,000.
My first question to the Minister of Finance on clause 1 is this. Could he tell us why his department has recommended that this change be made?

Mr. Chairman, it was to adjust the amount of money which was allocated in order to help the people or to give them more incentive to invest risk money so that they could be somewhat compensated for the losses incurred. There were a lot of representations made on that subject by various groups. Some would like the government to permit a deduction of all the losses, which we do not think is advisable. I think this scheme is a good one. Not only can a person deduct $2,000 from capital gains but he can also deduct it from general income. It is a good incentive for people to take some risk in order to develop the Canadian economy.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has indicated that his departmental officials feel it would not be desirable to allow all of the capital losses to be deducted. Would the minister indicate why that is felt? Why cannot a person deduct all of his capital losses against all of his capital gains?

Mr. Chairman, 1 think the main reason is that it would be much too expensive for the treasury; moreover, it might result in some inequities in our tax system. For those reasons, I think it would not be advisable at this time.

Mr. Chairman, 1 should like to explore that a little more. What would be the magnitude of the loss to the federal treasury if all capital losses were chargeable against all

November 25, 1977
Income Tax Act
capital gains? I ask this because it has always been represented by the department that this is not really a big money winner. The last time we inquired, capital gains tax was yielding approximately $70 billion or $80 billion of tax revenue. I am somewhat startled to find the minister using the rationale that if capital losses were permitted to be applied against capital gains, it would be just too big a loss as far as the treasury is concerned. Could the minister indicate more specifically what the estimated loss would be?

Mr. Chairman, that is not exactly what I said. We are not permitting the losses to be deducted only against capital gains, as is the case in the United Kingdom and the United States. We will permit the losses to be deducted against other income. In terms of how costly it will be, I am informed that this deduction of another $1,000, in terms of losses from income, will cost the treasury $45 million. It is difficult to assess exactly, if we permitted all the losses to be deducted from income, the amount of money we would lose, but it could be in the hundreds of millions of dollars. That is why we think that should not be done, and it is not called for either.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister misunderstood my question. I am well aware of what he said earlier. What would be the cost to the treasury if the British or American approach was accepted, thus allowing capital losses to be claimed against capital gains without any limit? What would be the loss then? 1 am not talking about all capital losses being claimed against income generally. How much would the loss be to the treasury if it was restricted to losses made on capital items being chargeable against any gains?
Mr. Chairman, I am informed that now they are deductible against capital gains fully, but not against income.

Mr. Chairman, I will put my question another way. Is the minister able to indicate to us what actualy has been the capital gains tax revenue which the treasury has been able to pocket in the last year, or the last time-frame within his knowledge?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: He is thinking.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar should be smart by smiling across the chamber. I do not pretend to have all those figures in my head.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I was talking to your colleague.
When I am asked how many hundreds of millions have been gained out of a tax like that, those figures are not in my head. It is $165 million, and $90 million on the corporate tax act.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to have more exact figures. Combined, how much total revenue has been gained, after all losses are accounted for and all deductions

have been allowed, by the federal treasury in the last year for which the minister has information available?
Mr. Chairman, in 1975 the total was $255 million.

Mr. Chairman, if I may, I should like to be able to reconcile those figures with the figures shown in the taxation statistics, 1977 edition. Perhaps after two o'clock I will have an opportunity to compare the $255 million figure that the minister has given us to the figures set out by the Department of National Revenue in that booklet. I should like to explore a more general subject dealing with capital gains. We have had, now, a few years experience with capital gains tax. Many people feel it is a grossly unfair tax, in the sense that there is no allowance made for inflation on items regarded as capital items. I know the government's stock answer is that it only takes 50 per cent of the gain-that is rough justice- and that somehow or other the eventual tax payable is not really confiscation of a person's assets.
Before getting into that, I should like to ask the minister the following: We have had some experience now with respect to indexing of income tax. What is the minister's general observation with regard to indexing? Does he feel it has been a good idea? Is it something that he feels is a step in the right direction?

In some aspects, yes, and in other aspects, no. Those are my feelings. It is a good concept in the sense that in some ways it will cope, in terms of taxation, with the inflation problems that we face in this counry. That is a positive element. The negative element is that if you compare Canadian taxation with that of other nations, for example, because it is automatic nobody realizes there is a tax cut.
For example, if I combine in my economic statement the tax cut that you have proposed, plus indexation, I am told that it is, relatively speaking, as great a tax cut as that called for by the so-called liberal democrats in the United States at this time. The drawback is that automatic indexing of 7.2 per cent for the next year is not considered by the public to be a tax cut, in terms of the economic definition in other nations. This is a drawback because, in fact, rather than announcing a tax cut of $700 million, as I have, on personal income tax for the year of 1978,1 would have one of $1.5 billion or $1.6 billion.
Psychologically, it would have a better impact if I were to do it the way it is done in the United States. I heard many speeches made in that context in the United States a few years ago. Relatively speaking, it is not more than we have done here, but because of the automatic indexing system we do not get the psychological impact we would have if it was announced as a new tax cut.

Mr. Chairman, if I may continue, I take it from the minister's remarks that he has no intention of modifying the indexing as far as income tax is concerned. Could he tell us specifically what the department now feels will be the
November 25, 1977

increment, if you like, of income tax as opposed to the increase in income itself? What leverage is there in the tax system as far as tax revenue is concerned in relation to the general growth of income in the country? At one time, before indexing, I believe it was estimated that federal government income tax went up somewhere between 1.7 per cent and 1.9 per cent in relation to the general increase in income. With indexing, what do they determine the federal tax increase to be in relation to rising income?
Mr. Chairman, this is a highly technical question, and I am not in a position to answer it right now. I will get the information and forward it to the hon. member later today.
Mr. Chairman, I would prefer the minister to give it to us this afternoon, because many people are interested and I think it should be in the record rather than just forwarded to me.

Mr. Chairman, my intention is to report to this Elouse because I can see in which direction the hon. member is going. J would not want to impute any motives to him but in the speeches we heard on second reading, some members of the opposition mentioned on several occasions that Canada was the most heavily taxed country in the world or at least of the western world.
That is right.
By the way, 1 want to say to the hon. member that he is wrong.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot speak for all members of this House, but I can speak for myself. The Minister of Finance is quite wrong in accusing me of having made the statement that we are the highest taxed.
Mr. Chairman, I want to say that it was not the hon. member whom I heard make that statement, but I have heard it a number of times from members of the opposition.

Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Chairman. Could we shift, then, from the indexing of income tax to the question of inflation in relation to capital gains? It is a self-evident fact that if you have invested $10,000 in capital investment to keep up with inflation, at present you would need, at the end of 12 months, about $10,880 just to stand still as far as your capital assets are concerned. However, with capital gains tax, if you liquidate you are deemed to have made $880, which is simply an inflationary increment, and you are taxed with respect to 50 per cent of that. My question to the minister is whether the government has been giving any consideration to some type of an indexing formula which
Income Tax Act
would ensure that gains on capital items which are offsetting inflationary gains should not, in fact, be taxed.

We have received many representations to that effect, and it is apparently an extremely difficult technical problem to resolve. You are talking about the capital gain of a person who is not, in fact, making that much of a capital gain because of inflation. He might have to pay as much as 25 per cent cent, for at least half of his rate. We are considering the problem, but we do not have any intention at this time of changing the present system.

There are two points that I would like to raise, Mr. Chairman. The minister has been told by his officials, as I noticed, that it is very complicated. I ask the same officials to advise him why it is so complicated. You know what your purchase price is, and we have a consumer price index that could report what, in fact, is the CPI on that date. When you choose a date to sell, surely the index will still be as useful to determine what, in fact, has been the rate of inflation. In short, you simply index each property in accordance with when you purchased it and when you decided to sell. Perhaps I will give the minister an opportunity to reply to that question first.

If everything were to be done on a yearly basis and in a very clear fashion as you report your income tax each year, that would be fine. However, you can buy a piece of land and sell it some weeks later. You can buy a share on January 19 and decide to sell it a few days later and calculate the inflation in between, and so on. It is a difficult problem with many, many transactions, and there are millions of transactions.
If all transactions were made in a fixed period, it would be quite possible, and we can do that in terms of fixed income because the salaries are paid and you calculate your income at the end of the year. But there are a lot of transactions that are done in short periods of time, and it is extremely complicated, according to the experts who look into that. However, I have listened to the representations of the hon. member, and we have received other representations to that effect, but we have come to the conclusion that it would not be appropriate to do that at this time.

Mr. Chairman, again to the minister. I am wondering if the minister would agree that, in the example I gave of a person who has bought capital items amounting to $10,000 a year ago and, sells them for $10,880, he is simply selling them, in constant dollars, at exactly the same price he paid for them initially. Would the minister not agree that any tax on that increment of $880 is confiscation of a man's capital goods? It does not matter if you tax 50 per cent of it, or 10 per cent; the fact is that in real dollars, expressed as 1976 dollars, the man has made no gain, yet the federal treasury is deeming a gain to have been made and is taxing him. Is that not confiscation?

If one wants to debate the principle of taxation, I have met people who claim that all taxes are confiscation. You can argue that forever. When income tax

November 25, 1977
Income Tax Act
was first started, people could have argued that any taxes are confiscation. I feel taxes are a way to operate a modern economy, and all taxes are creating a burden on some people. In fact, rather than a gain, you would have a loss because you would know when you bought the shares that you needed to make enough money to cover the taxes on their sale. He knew, when he bought the shares, that he needed to make enough money because there was a tax to pay, and he had a loss rather than a gain; that is all.

I would think the minister would agree that there is a very clear distinction between the example I am giving and the general feeling that any tax revenue you have to contribute is confiscation. In the example I have given, if we were to take it in a series the man, in fact, would have no money left after simply buying and selling an asset. He tried to keep up with inflation but constantly was taxed.
We could work it out, but certainly if you did for 15 or 20 years what I have indicated, buying $1,000 and selling it at a value just enough to equal your current inflation, and then rebuying but paying the tax in the meantime, you would virtually have no assets left. I think the insidious thing about this type of tax is the fact that it is confiscation of capital at the very time this nation needs huge capital investment in order to create the jobs we need for those who are out of work. In that sense, would the minister agree that there is a clear distinction when we are dealing with the possible confiscation of capital and the growth of capital compared with other taxation?

We could go inio a long debate on the philosophical implications of taxation, and so forth. We decided to tax capital gains some years ago. It was somewhat controversial, but we decided that because it was a capital gain we would tax it at only half the rate because there is an element of risk. The hon. member knows that because of this risk we decided not to consider it normal income. The hon. member will remember the proposition in the Carter report that a buck is a buck whether it is earned by capital or as part of a salary.
However, we decided that because there was an element of risk we would tax at half the rate, and that is part of the gain. We know that in some cases a case can be made, just as the hon. member is making a case now. I explained earlier the complexity of trying to be just in every situation. So far we have not found the formula. There are some aspects of the argument of the hon. member which are valid; I have to concede that. There are some problems with these tax changes.
Every time we try to be nice to everybody, we make it so complicated that taxpayers do not understand how to deal with their tax forms, and in this case a problem which already exists will be further complicated. I recognize that there is a problem, but this matter involves risk. If people get just the equivalent of inflation, there has to be a reconciliation because of the tax system in Canada. In this situation, people did not

break even; they suffered losses. That is why we made an allocation for losses in the tax system.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member has had more than 20 minutes of questions and answers. I must see another hon. member, but I will come back to the hon. member for York-Simcoe later.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to this exchange with great interest. It is a very important exchange. I very much agreed with the hon. member for York-Simcoe when he talked about the danger of capital losses. Because I am always willing to be very helpful to both sides of this House-the minister has indicated how complex the whole thing is and that he is looking for a simplified and just way, which he has not found-I think there is a just and simple way. It is the way the Carter commission suggested.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe has a good argument about the effect of inflation on capital, and surely it should not be the purpose of a tax system, in our present philosophy, to wipe out the actual capital of a person. The answer should have been obvious. I think it is very simple, and I hope the hon. member for York-Simcoe will agree. Then we could go arm in arm to the Minister of Finance since he seems to be amenable to suggestions and to simplifying things. We might, in fact, get the taxation system changed along this line.
I would like to suggest to the hon. member for York-Simcoe that we agree to a full capital gains tax which is indexed for inflation. That is very, very simple. Capital gains could be taxed at the same rate as ordinary income, with indexation for inflation, which would retain the value of the capital. It seems to me that that would simplify the whole tax system. We could then go on from there.
I really need to hear from the hon. member for York-Simcoe whether he agrees with that kind of proposal. Justice would be done, because if we tax capital gains at their full value we get around this whole business of arguing whether it should be one-quarter, one-half or one-third, and then we assure those who do have capital that there will be no loss of their assets as a result of inflation.
I would be generous even to the point of saying that if it is bought and sold at different times of the year, it should be taken to the nearest year, allowing the benefit of that particular year's indexing, rather than the other way around. That seems to be a very simple proposition to which all of us might perhaps agree. That would restore the element of justice Carter was talking about in his report, that all income should be treated the same. I must say that my suggestion does not seem to be greeted with any wild enthusisasm. I thought it was a very good suggestion. I thought I was trying to be very helpful. Oh, I see I have the support of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

First time he has ever agreed with you.
November 25, 1977

Not really. He has agreed with me on many occasions, and I value his judgment highly. I am glad to get endorsation from such an august authority.
Mr. Chairman, I do not expect we are going to get agreement on that, but since the question of indexing has been raised, I want to say something about that and leave it to the minister to comment. As the minister says, we can say good things and bad things about indexing. I just proposed one kind of indexing which I think is a very valid kind of indexing because it is a guarantee of indexing on capital. However, other kinds of indexing are equally valid. I certainly support the indexing of family allowances and old age pensions. I think that is important, particularly because we are dealing with people who do not have a way of recouping any losses from inflation in the way that most people who are in the labour market have some ability to do that. Because they are universal things, therefore everybody benefits to the same extent.
The minister has made some arguments for the indexing of income tax. He has also made some arguments against it. 1 have an argument which is very much against it, in the light of experience. I believe many of my colleagues supported the notion of indexing income tax as a way of ensuring some offset against inflation. I think the assumption was that our income tax system would be getting more and more progressive, and therefore indexing would not have the effect we now see it to have.
One of the consequences of indexing the minister has not dealt with is that it tends to help those in higher income brackets to a greater extent than those in lower income brackets, because of the percentage application that is made, which means that that element of social and economic policy is removed from debate. I think to that extent indexing has resulted in making our whole tax system more regressive than it need be. For that reason, I would be inclined to agree that indexing of the tax system has outlived its usefulness. The idea of visibility is terribly important, to this extent: we live in a society where there is hardly anyone who does not have a grievance. Everybody thinks he is hard done by. All these automatic benefits are built in, and while there is something to be said for them, they are not as visible as they should be.
It seems to me that if we are to understand our system somewhat better than we do now, more and more of the benefits that have been built in and taken for granted should be visible. This has certainly been the argument of my party on the tax system, and it will be the argument we put forward as this debate progresses. I am not putting this to the minister in the form of a question, because he has dealt with it- although, of course, if he cares to comment, he is free to do so. Instead, I intend to go into the clause by clause examination that we are prepared for.
Before doing that, however, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister something that I propose to use in the clause by clause examination. I was fortunate enough to receive a series of critiques of the clauses from Professor Neil
Income Tax Act
Brooks of York University, prepared by his students at Osgoode Hall Law School. The letter states in part:
In particular, I would be very interested in your view on how such comments might be presented to be of more use to you and other MPs. I hope to have the students prepare comments on all future tax bills. Indeed in future semesters, we will be devoting more time to such a project. This semester we are doing as well another major project on tax reform.
It strikes me that this is an excellent idea. While these students may not be as expert as the minister's advisers, they are working in this field in a very serious manner. Because they can concentrate on each clause, they can provide some excellent advice and at least a different point of view. I have not answered the letter yet, but in a way I am answering it publicly. Not only do I feel that this critique will be of great help to me and other members, but I think the practice should continue. If any member would like a copy, it will be available. I do not intend to clutch it to my bosom or to keep it for my colleagues alone. I presume Professor Brooks intended it should be available to any member who chooses to use the information prepared in this way.
Not only will I be answering Professor Brooks by what I am doing, and stating my views on the critique, but the students will be able to see it in perhaps better from in Hansard. In that way, they will be able to see the extent to which their work has been used in this House. Personally, I am very grateful for the interest shown by this class at Osgoode Hall, and I intend to read into the record and base questions upon some of the studies conducted by the students. I use that as a preamble, Mr. Chairman, lest someone thinks this esoteric knowledge comes out of my own head and that the great and valuable research was done in my office.
Regarding clause 1, the paper notes as follows:
1.	The policy reason for not allowing individuals to offset allowable capital losses against ordinary income is sound. Capital gains are only taxed when realized. Thus, it would be possible for an individual to time his capital gains and losses to minimize tax. For example, he could realize his gains in years of low income and his losses in years of high income. To prevent this timing of gains and losses, capital losses are generally only deductible from capital gains.
2.	Two reasons can be suggested for the creation of the "$1,000 rule" which allows a partial offset of capital losses against other income.
(a)	It tends to decrease the down-side risk when investing in capital property. The purchaser of stocks, for example, is afforded some relief from a loss because he can deduct it to some extent from other income.
(b)	It provides some relief for taxpayers with little capital property; i.e. the person who might suffer a capital loss yet never incur a capital gains against which to offset the loss.
3.	Do present conditions justify increasing the capital loss offset figure?
(a) Consonant with the proposed aims outlined in the budget speech (p. 12), the Liberal government is attempting to increase purchases in the equity market by offering the average Canadian investment incentives by way of a larger write-off of capital losses against ordinary income. Tables found in the budget supplementary papers (p. 4) show that $45 million will be lost by the government in the first year of the provision's enactment, with an additional $5 million forfeited in 1978.
While the government has calculated the costs of implementation, it has no idea of the increased investment which the measure is supposed to stimulate or the extent to which it will encourage people to further bunch their losses in order to gain the benefit of the write-off. If this be the justification for increasing the amount of the offset, the government should have determined whether a sufficient increase in equity investment would take place in order to justify a loss of $45 million.

November 25, 1977
Income Tax Act
(b) For the last few years, inflation has eaten away at the value of the dollar.
Consequently, losses of $1,000 Five years ago are losses of a greater amount
today. The capital loss offset may have been doubled in order to combat
inflation. A prudent and more logical alternative would have been simply to
index the present sum by the present rate of inflation.
4.	Even though it may appear arbitrary, the figure of $2,000 was not chosen at random. In increasing the amount permitted for capital loss offset, the Liberal government has followed the lead of the United States once more, having previously borrowed the "$1,000 rule" from the IRS Code. The Tax Reform Bill of 1976 provides for the increase of the capital loss offset figure to $2,000 in 1977 and $3,000 in 1978 and subsequent years. Based on the government's past method of choosing its figure for capital loss offset and its failure to conduct a cost-benefit analysis as to the merits of the proposal, it is surprising that the proposed changes do not advocate the institution of a "$3,000 rule" in 1978.
The question that arises is a very straightforward one of cost benefit. According to the best figures we have, it will result in a $45 million revenue loss to the government. In order to justify this kind of loss, we need to know if studies have been carried out and alternatives examined. For example, would $45 million be better invested directly in incentives to industry, in regional development, in direct job creation, or in public works, than in what has become a sort of traditional way when the government tries to stimulate employment by spreading money around without knowing the consequences of the spread?
If past experience is any guide, when incentives are offered to industry through the tax system and in other ways, increased investment in jobs will not necessarily result. My specific question to the minister, therefore, is whether studies have been made to determine alternate means of spending that $45 million to see if more jobs could be created or more equity created in some other way.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot give a specific answer about particular studies, and so on. This is the collective judgment of the administration, and the money is needed in the economy at this time to stimulate risk investment. We must induce Canadians to put more money into risk ventures because we believe jobs cannot all be created by the public sector. The private sector is the one that creates the most jobs.
In giving that added incentive, we are very confident that a number of Canadians will want to channel their money into risk-buying rather than purchasing bonds, having a completely secure investment, which was the thing to do. We are confident of that. We have received many representations to the effect that we should give more incentive to the people so they can make that kind of investment, which is exactly the same proposition which my predecessor, the hon. member for Rose-dale, made to the House of Commons.

A little while ago the minister made a statement outside of the House, saying that Canadians may be saving too much and the consequences of that may not be good for the economy. The minister agreed he made that statement and he is concerned about that matter. This need to grant additional benefits to investors in the stock market is bothersome and arises as a direct result of the government's policy to encourage savings and to provide benefits for those who put

their money into bonds and into registered retirement savings plans-in the very sort of safe instruments he is now worried about.
Having now created the Frankenstein of encouraging savings in the safe sector, in the sector that has virtually no risk, he finds that by encouraging people to put money into the safe sector, then you have to find some way of giving them more if they go into the unsafe sector, the risky sector. Rather than recognizing where the problem is at its source, he has overencouraged savings and money into the safe sector. He simply says we now have to offset it by giving more benefits than we perhaps wanted to give in order to encourage people to begin to take risks again.
I do not disagree with the minister, Mr. Chairman, that we are living in a society which, certainly for the foreseeable future, will be dependent on the private sector for providing jobs. Anything we can do which would be effective-I emphasize the word "effective"-to provide those jobs is something my colleagues would certainly agree to. This is the problem. Why, in the minister's view, is it-and I am not quarrelling with him-that those who take risks should in some way be somewhat encouraged to take risks; because even if we lived another kind of society, risk-taking would still be necessary.
If the private sector does not do it, governments have to do it. Governments have to take risks in the sense of the public works they engage in. There are no guarantees that even the public works are going to be free of risks. The question I would like the minister to answer is this. Instead of building on this silly superstructure which the government has created by encouraging safe savings to a point where savings have become, perhaps, the most serious problem in our society in terms of trying to get economic development which encourages consumption, why would the minister not back off from some of the safe savings proposals that he brought in? In that way he would not have to be faced with this business of giving away $45 million in order to hopefully, encourage people to take additional risks, and there is no evidence that it will in fact happen.
Would you kindly repeat the question for me, please?

I just want to make the point that we have demonstrated the utility of parliamentary assistants: they pay more attention to the debate than the minister does. I realize the minister is sitting with a most interesting former minister of finance who has heard my voice before and perhaps can anticipate some of the questions I am raising. My question is this: Rather than increase the benefits and lose the $45 million that is going to be lost in the tax system, through this particular measure in clause 1, to encourage people to take risks, why did he not reduce the incentive to save which, on his own analysis, is one of the problems?
Why did he not reduce those incentives? In that way the differential between the rewards for risk-taking and for those who do not take risks would have continued. Why did he not do it the other way, rather than give away this amount of
November 25, 1977

money and still continue a system which has demonstrated that it is resulting in too much savings?

I am learning a little listening to the hon. member, but I am learning much more by listening to the former minister of finance, my good colleague from Eglinton who has been an extremely useful member of this House. I will not apologize, because he was giving me some good advice.
Hear, hear!

To answer your question, we are talking about two different things. It is a question of judgment. We have decided to go along with this system of changing the amount of money that can be deducted from income, from losses, in order to stimulate the economy. That is the direction we have chosen. The incentive for savings is a completely different problem. Some people are saving too much, but that does not mean that we should not save as a nation. We should not be confused there.
As I said the other day, some people should start to spend some of their money because savings have been very high for the last three years. For some people we have special programs of savings; for example, the people who are saving for retirement purposes. I think this is a natural thing to do. We have another scheme, the home ownership desired by the young people. They eventually want to own their own home. That is a form of savings to be kept. This is our judgment. I can see the frustration of the hon. member, because he is from the NDP and he knows that he will never have to make those judgments.
You never know.
I heard that once in Saskatchewan.

I am quite prepared to consent, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext: 1 have no objection. I saw the hon. member for Calgary North rise a few times and I was ready to recognize him, but nothing prevents me from allowing the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge to pursue his questioning if no other member rises in between each question.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 1 appreciate the generosity of the hon. member. I was going to say that normally I appreciate the comments of the minister, but in this case I did not appreciate them at all. With respect to the comment about the NDP, I would rather be here in the opposition, without the opportunity he has, than be held responsible for the kind of mess that his government has got this country into.
Hear, hear!

It could be worse.

I do not see how it could be worse. You would have to stay up nights to try to figure out how to wreck an economy the way this government has. It is quite obvious what is happening. The minister talks about different problems. They are not different problems. He talks about it being our judgment. In face of the fact that your judgment has been pretty awful, is it not about time you changed your judgment or changed the people who are advising you? This really should be obvious to the minister, if it is not obvious to anyone else. I certainly think it is obvious to many people.
There are other comments I could make. I appreciate the generosity of the committee in giving me this time. 1 do not normally like to participate in this kind of personal banter. However, the minister does not have much of a stand from which he can point his finger at other people and be critical of their behaviour.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to engage in a political debate, but I cannot let that go. There are too many people who take pleasure in saying how bad things are in Canada. Of course, we have not been perfect as a government. We do not claim that. However, look at the programs which have been introduced in the past 15 years. Since I came to this House, many social programs have been put into effect in Canada, to the point that the hon. member sometimes claims-
It was the effectiveness of the NDP in the minority government.
Having served in this House for the past 15 years, I am proud of the progress that has been made in spite of the gloom and doom we have heard from the other side for all those years.

Mr. Chairman, we are sitting as a committee of the whole House, as was done under the former rules. This is done particularly on tax measures. I want to discuss capital gains, particularly as they affect small business people, smallholders in the cities, the farmers and the oil and gas industry. Before discussing capital gains, there is something else I have to say. The job of the tax collectors in the Department of National Revenue is very difficult. Very often these people are seeking information. They must take certain steps in order to keep their records in shape, and must ensure that taxpayers pay their proper and equitable share of tax.
Through my associations as a lawyer, I have dealt with many people in the Department of National Revenue. I wish to compliment them. They do not have an easy job. The personnel in the city of Calgary are always polite, courteous and helpful. If there is some difficulty or dispute as to the interpretation of the act or the value of a property, they will sit down with the taxpayer and work it out in a proper, compromising way. I want to pay that compliment because too often the personnel in the department are criticized. It is in the every day

November 25, 1977
Income Tax Act
working with citizens that the goodwill has built up in my city. I can only speak of my home city.
I also want to discuss capital gains. I say this nicely, even to my good friends in the NDP. I know we take the same position when the government gets into serious economic trouble and there is unemployment. We were the government of this country in the thirties when there was a world depression. We also had difficulty during the years of the right hon. member for Prince Albert. It is not always easy to come to the right decision. When you hear people talk about raising more taxes for grandiose things, you should remember who brought in capital gains. Edgar Benson and Pat Mahoney of Calgary- and he was defeated for this reason-piloted through this House, for the first time, a capital gains tax. I raised my voice against it.
One of the causes of economic destruction and distress in this country is that 50 per cent of capital gains is added to the top of your income, like the icing on the cake. If you are in the 30 per cent or 40 per cent bracket, you are put into another bracket. Capital gains are treated like any other income. We heard in this morning's question period that there is a lot less unemployment in the United States. I have relatives living in that country. In fact, my sister lives in San Francisco. I figured out what my tax would have been last year had I lived in the United States. It would have been 30 per cent to 40 per cent less on capital gains. That is because in Canada it is added on the top of your income.
In the United States you can go to the department to find out what your tax will be. It is a set tax of 25 per cent, with some rules and regulations for different kinds of property. If we had a reasonable and equitable capital gains tax, it would help the businessmen, the factories, the farmers and the oil and gas industry. We would not have such a high rate of unemployment in Newfoundland. It would help the people there.

I appreciate your humour, but this is too serious a matter for nonsense. Coming back to capital gains, in addition to helping those people it would create jobs. There would be increased exploration and development in oil and gas. The farmer in Ontario would have more money to purchase machinery. More jobs would be available in the factories of Ontario. People could buy more consumer goods such as cars, refrigerators and farm machinery. By taking it off the top, you crush the capital flow. That is what has brought about economic collapse and chaos in this country. I refer to the bill brought in and piloted by Mr. Benson. The treasury benches today are reaping the sins of the Trudeau government of 1968, 1969 and 1970.
Supposing a person who owns a small plot of land wants to sell that land. He must go back to "V" day, valuation day. The difference between that and what the department determines to be the value on the day of the sale is the amount on which you pay tax. You go to the land titles office to get a certified copy of the transfer, to show the valuation. Along comes the

department and says that their appraiser has a different figure. Therefore, you must hire an appraiser. I was told by one tax department official-I will not name the area-that the government spent $16,000 for an appraiser in order to try to collect $3,000 more tax.

speechtext: Order. When the committee rose at one o'clock, clause 1 of Bill C-11 was under consideration and the hon. member for Calgary North had the floor.

Mr. Chairman, just before the lunch hour I was dealing with capital gains. I want to bring to the attention of this committee that when the Income Tax Act was changed in the days of Benson and Pat Mahoney from Calgary South, my home city, who was defeated on the bill, I thought the government had acted with some wisdom in abolishing succession duties and death duties. But the government went on to implement a capital gains tax, and this tax differs from similar taxes in other western nations. Under our law, capital gains are treated in the same way as other income. So whatever one's salary or income is, if a small businessman, say, sells a little piece of property and there is a capital gain, 50 per cent of that gain is taxable at the same rate as his income is taxed.
I was saying before lunch that there is a capital gains tax in the United States, which we must remember is an older industrial nation than ours. At the time the government introduced the capital gains tax, I said it would stop exploration for gas and oil. I also said it would affect the small businessman and the farmer. If you add all that together, Mr. Chairman, the growth of the country itself is affected, and without growth you have unemployment. If you inhibit capital flow-income flow, as it were-how can small businessmen, farmers or manufacturers grow, and how can oil and gas corporations conduct exploration for gas and oil and develop their business? When you stop growth because of overtaxed enterprises on the part of government, you bring about no growth and, as I say, no growth creates unemployment.
On the day that this voluminous bill which changed the income tax structure of this nation received royal assent, growth in this nation, whether growth of industry, farming operations or oil and gas or mining companies, started to decline. With that decline in growth, unemployment increased. This is where I fall out with my good friends, the members of the New Democratic Party. They always say that we must have a high capital gains tax; but once we have a tax structure like the one we have today in Canada, we might as well go all
November 25, 1977

the way and have the state own everything, because it really amounts to that.
I want to deal with how this tax affects the small businessman. Take the case of the little corner store. A businessman buys such a store, the lot, the stock and equipment, and so on. Then after spending 13 or 14 hours a day in that store for seven or eight years, with his wife assisting him, too, he feels that he should retire because he has worked hard. When he puts his business up for sale, the lot has increased in price and he has to pay tax on 50 per cent of the capital gain that he makes on the lot, in addition to his income tax. In other words, progressive tax is not only progressive with regard to income; it is also progressive with regard to capital gains.
In the United States, the tax is fixed at 25 per cent; it cannot go higher. In this country, you do not have to make much money to get into the 50 per cent to 60 per cent bracket. A 50 per cent to 60 per cent tax on a capital gain, with inflation today, takes away the savings of a small grocer. This is why we must have an increase in pensions. You cannot have it both ways.
Now let me talk about another factor I mentioned before lunch. The owner of a small store says that in January, 1972, his land was worth $10,000. Perhaps if he sells it now it will be worth $15,000. Perhaps he obtains the transfer of a similar property close by. This might happen in any part of the country. The department might very well not accept that valuation and will hire its own appraiser to appraise the property. The department can do this, because money is no obstacle. The department will often spend $16,000 in order to collect $4,000 in taxes. When the taxpayer goes to the tax department, he is told that the department has an appraiser's report which indicates a certain value. The taxpayer might not agree with that value, and is told by the department to hire his own appraiser. If he does, he may be stuck with the cost, perhaps amounting to $1,000 or $1,600. Even if he wins the battle, he has to pay that amount.
Let me now talk about the situation in which farmers on the prairies find themselves. If a farmer sells his land, or rolls it over to his son-and we can thank the hon. member for Halifax for this legislation which was brought in when he was the national leader of this party-the land passes from the father to the son, or even to the grandson, and that tax is deferred. However, it has to be paid some day, by the last survivor, when the land is sold.
However, when we changed the rules the situation became entirely different. Perhaps a farmer would form a small personal company or corporation which included his son and his wife. Following that, he might decide to retire or sell his shares. The situation would not be the same as selling the land to his son, and the rule of rolling over the land from father to son would not apply. The individual had set up a corporation before the tax law came in; but what the governments have done-and I am speaking of them in the plural-is change the rules in midstream, and they then wonder why business is
Income Tax Act
disrupted and there is little growth. They ask why there is unemployment. I suggest this is one good reason for unemployment.
Let me put the point in another way. If the farmer formed a small personal corporation before the change, it would meet the rules, making it much easier to transfer shares in the land, and at a savings on the death of the farmer. That is the situation if the corporation was formed before the tax change. If he should now liquidate his corporation and pass the land on, he must pay the capital gains tax. What manner of nonsense is this? This is the government which brought that law into being. As the member for Calgary North, I spoke for days criticizing the action of this government, but they just laughed it off, said my criticism meant nothing and rammed the legislation through. That is why the hon. member for Edmonton Centre took the tax bill, tore it in half and threw it on the floor, saying, "This is what you have done to Canada". I remember the night when the tax measures were rammed through by closure. I wish the members of this government would cross the country and talk to the people at the grass roots, to find out what they think about our income tax laws and how they are treated as taxpayers.
Let me discuss another industry which is dear to the heart of all Calgarians and Edmontonians, because practically every job in the cities of Calgary and Edmonton is based directly or indirectly on agriculture or on oil and gas. It was not by accident that the government of Alberta discovered oil and gas there. Premier Manning had a fine government: I have always said that. He encouraged capital investment on the part of foreign companies, giving them a chance to make a dollar on their investment.
I think Imperial Oil drilled 90 dry holes in Alberta before striking oil. I wonder how many here know what it cost to drill a well even back in those days. I suggest it cost about $600,000 then and about $1.6 million now. While that was taking place, drilling rigs were pulling out of Saskatchewan from all over because of that province's tax structure. That government believed in socialism, whereas the Alberta government believed in business and enterprise. Therein lies the difference.
We are now facing a very serious situation when dealing with capital gains and business taxes. Let me refer to the judgment handed down recently in the case of Canadian Industrial Gas and Oil Limited v. The Government of Saskatchewan. When the world price of oil went up, the Saskatchewan government said the price had to be maintained at $4.50 per barrel. It demanded that any increase would go entirely to the government no matter what happened to the cost of production. I think this recent judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada is one of the most important to be handed down in recent years. It will affect not only that province but the province of Ontario, where nickel is exported, and any other province which exports products such as oil, gas, wheat, or what have you. Let me read a short extract from this judgment as follows:
It is contended that both the mineral income tax and the royalty surcharge constitute indirect taxation, and are therefore beyond the power of the province

to impose, the provincial legislative powers being limited to direct taxation within the province under subs. 92(2) of the British North America Act.
It is contended that the legislation relates to the regulation of interprovincial and international trade and commerce, a matter over which the federal parliament has exclusive legislative power-
This legislation will have serious ramifications in eastern Canada because of exportation. With this kind of taxation and law, what will happen to growth in this vigorous nation? Because of the serious ramifications of this decision in respect of provincial control of resources, and particularly in view of the thin strings of confederation, I would ask the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister to bring the provinces together to discuss this matter and find a solution once and for all. Let me say to the people in the east that although they may think this only relates to oil and gas, it relates to all exported products.
Let us consider the nickel industry. This is a commodity that is exported. The tax will be applied in that case. People are wondering why mining companies are closing down and why there are so many lay-offs. They wonder why the companies are struggling to keep the mines open. My friends to the left have been talking about unemployment and lay-offs in the mines, and quite rightly so. 1 suggest that this situation is the result of the tax structure in this country. Because of this tax structure, these mines cannot make a profit. The government keeps trying to get the last dollar possible from these companies in the form of taxes, forcing the companies to close because they can no longer make a profit. This results in unemployment. It is a vicious circle.
This country's tax laws should be the subject of immediate review. It is almost impossible to think we can have so much unemployment in a country so rich in resources of all kinds. I suggest this is the only country in the world which until the last few years had problems only in relation to surpluses. Let us consider the situation in countries which have shortages. This country has a surplus of resources, many of them still waiting to be tapped and developed. As an hon. member from Newfoundland said today, that is a province with great resources waiting to be tapped, yet business is struggling to stay alive because of government taxes, including capital gains and high, progressive rates. Business just cannot be done in these circumstances and there is bound to be unemployment.
We have a monstrous tax structure in this country that is stifling growth, killing industry, creating unemployment, economic chaos and other problems which Canada faces today. This government should get together a strong committee made up of businessmen, union leaders and others across the nation to study the tax structure. I am sure such a committee would find that overtaxation is responsible for most of the economic ills of the nation. Let such a committee get on with the job of reviewing the tax structure, instead of the government always trying to figure out how to get the last dollar from the people of Canada. If the government continues with that approach, we will never have full growth or full employment. I see that my time has expired. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments to address myself to the consequences that flow from the tax policies of this government, whether by way of tax incentives, capital gains tax, industrial incentives or any other kind of incentive under the Regional Development Incentives Act. The fact of the matter is that we have to create a climate in this country to develop the vast undeveloped resources of Canada as a first priority toward tackling what has to be the first priority, namely, unemployment.
Today, in the Atlantic provinces, there is an unemployment rate which exceeds that which is faced by industrial states elsewhere in the western world. The figures speak for themselves. For October, 1977, the unemployment rate in Newfoundland was 17.4 per cent, which is a substantial increase from last year. Still referring to October, 1977, the unemployment rate in New Brunswick was 14.6 per cent; in Nova Scotia, 10.7 per cent; and in Prince Edward Island, 11.2 per cent. For the Atlantic region as a whole, the unemployment rate was 13.5 per cent. Those figures do not tell the true story. They are seasonally adjusted, which is the strange, indefinable, incomprehensible methodology of Statistics Canada for measuring unemployment.
To arrive at the real rate of unemployment one must look at the number of recipients who are drawing unemployment insurance. One of the first qualifications for unemployment benefits is that the recipient has to be unemployed and available for work. Using the unemployment insurance program, the welfare rolls and the real method of measurement, one can arrive at the real situation.
I should like to refer to some percentages which are underestimates, for the month of October. In the province of Newfoundland the real unemployment rate was 27.6 per cent, or
60.000	people; in the province of Prince Edward Island, it was 20 per cent, or 11,000 people; in the province of Nova Scotia it was 15.5 per cent, or 55,000 people; and in New Brunswick it was 20.7 per cent, or 61,000 people. The real unemployment total for the four provinces during the month of October was
187.000	people. Considering the loss of productivity to this country, the drain on the unemployment insurance fund and the drain on the already overburdened exchequers of those provinces, in terms of what it costs for unemployment insurance benefits, is enormous.
I am glad the Minister of Employment and Immigration is present in the chamber. According to Statistics Canada, 40 per cent of those looking for work in Atlantic Canada as of October, 1977, had been unemployed for longer than three months. I consider that to be monumental. Winter is coming, and the unemployed will be further aggravated. They will go into the winter only to have their unemployment benefits expire. Thus, unemployed workers drawing benefits at the present time will have no alternative but to go through the humiliation of a means test and apply for welfare through their provincial agencies. The greatest potential for social unrest in this country would be in my region.

In terms of youth unemployment, again there are startling statistics for the month of October, 1977. In the four Atlantic provinces it was 20.6 per cent, as opposed to 16.7 per cent of unemployed youth a year ago. What has happened in the way of job creation? Using StatCan's figures for October once again, there was last year a net increase in employment of 6,000. However, that 6,000 has to be shown in contrast to the growth in the labour force, which was some 20,000 in the same year. Thus, job creation has lagged behind in the Atlantic region, during the past year, by some 14,000 jobs. Let the Minister of Employment and Immigration reconcile his job creation programs to that fact, notwithstanding that these programs help to alleviate some of the hardships which accrue because of this disastrous situation.
The Prime Minister was in Newfoundland yesterday. It has the highest rate of unemployment in the country, and indeed any state in the western hemisphere. What was the Prime Minister's reaction when he was confronted by an orderly and peaceful demonstration of unemployed? It can only be likened to the petulance of Marie Antoinette when she was faced with a mob in Paris saying, "We have no bread", and she said, "Eat cake". That is what the Prime Minister said, "If you do not want the equalization grants, we will take them back". As one man said during that demonstration yesterday, "We do not want welfare; we want work". That is the case.
The province of Newfoundland has the potential to generate enough jobs for its people. Also, it has enough potential in the way of resources to assist the region and the country as a whole. That province has been blessed with an abundance of natural resources. It is the greatest producer of iron ore in Canada and has contributed substantially to Canada's balance of payments program. Also, Newfoundland is the greatest producer of hydropower, with a substantially undeveloped hydroelectric resource at Churchill Falls. It cannot be developed because the province does not have the financial capacity. Approximately 40 per cent of Quebec's power is generated from Newfoundland. There is enough undeveloped power to satisfy not only the needs of the province of Newfoundland in the foreseeable future but to satisfy the needs, to a large extent, of the energy-hungry Atlantic region as a whole.
What about the power going into Quebec? Today it is going in at approximately three mills. The market rate for that power is approximately 20 mills. If Newfoundland was receiving market prices, it would not have to go to the money markets of the world to cover its current account deficit at the present time.
From time to time we have appealed to the government to exercise its constitutional right, which is its authority under the British North America Act, to build transmission lines to make it possible for Newfoundland's power to get to the Ontario grid. What about the national grid we have heard about for years? It has been just talk. It would take approximately $2 billion to develop the lower Churchill, yet this government has not changed its attitude toward participating in that program over the last two or three years, notwithstanding the toll which has been taken by inflation. The offer of the
Income Tax Act
federal government still stands at about $3 hundred million in terms of development capital to get that vast, undeveloped hydro resource on stream to help this energy-hungry country of ours.
What about the vast potential of our fisheries? Well, the Minister of Finance today, in response to my question, talked about one of the initiatives the government has undertaken with regard to the economy of Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces with the imposition of the 200-mile limit. Sir, they had to be dragged kicking and screaming to sign that unilateral declaration for a 200-mile limit, and it was only after a number of bilateral agreements had been signed with a number of the countries that have had traditional, historic and treaty rights to the great Pacific and Atlantic Fishing grounds.
Sir, what have we been doing with that resource since we imposed a 200-mile limit? We have been bartering it away and allowing some of the countries of eastern Europe and the Caribbean, Cuba especially, to exploit quotas in certain species because we do not have the capacity at the present time to exploit all of our quotas within the 200-mile limit under our international agreement. So we barter away the unexploited quotas, and in the process we barter away future job opportunities for Canadians in that part of the country. It is done without reference to the province concerned. It is done unilaterally, as so many things are done by this government, without so much as a "by your leave", without so much as a consultation with the province that is to be affected. Of course, the province most affected in my area involving the fisheries near the Atlantic, obviously, is the province of Newfoundland where we are dependent on the fisheries, which is our first and prime resource.
Sir, I can go on to the timber resources in Newfoundland, second only to the vast timber resources of British Columbia, but which remain largely unexploited in the Labrador portion of the province. The potential is there for vast job creation possibilities, yet these timber resources are standing there rotting or being eaten away by various pests. We are a rich province, heavily endowed with mineral resources, hydroelectric resources, fishery resources, timber resources, resources of our people. In all, there are only 500,000 people in the province of Newfoundland.
I had my eyes opened a few years ago when I had occasion to visit Iceland, the independent republic of Iceland, with half the population of Newfoundland yet with so much in common with us. With half our population, they have an economy largely dependent on the same North Atlantic fishery that is so important to us. What have they been able to achieve with the proper exploitation and protection of that resource? Sir, they have been able to achieve full employment and have, probably, the fourth highest standard of living in the world.
Is it any wonder that our people are beginning to wonder about the approach to the concept of confederation by this government, this "rich man, poor man" approach so arrogantly expressed in St. John's yesterday by the Prime Minister?
