We are not content to be looked upon as parasites in confederation. We will not be content to be the recipient of the crumbs off the table of the rich provinces, because we are a rich province. I realize, sir, that we cannot put a price tag on confederation because this country will not survive unless there is a spirit of nationalism within the country.
By the same token, neither will this country survive if any single province within the country is not given the right to develop its full potential, which is one of the essential roles of this government. I worry, Mr. Chairman, about the long-term consequences of unemployment, what it does to all our people, including our young people. The unproductivity represented by the disastrous unemployment figures that are released monthly by Statistics Canada shows no sign of improvement.
We wonder how it is possible for the government of Canada, through its Export Development Corporation, to finance offshore corrugated cardboard plants in the United States, when the Labrador linerboard mill in western Newfoundland is forced to close its doors, putting 2,100 Canadians out of work. And who cares? We wonder about the fluorspar mine in St. Lawrence, Newfoundland, forced to close after 40 years of production during which the Aluminum Company of Canada made vast profits. We do not deny them profits, but they just callously closed their doors and walked way. Why? Because they get the same fluorspar in Mexico, with cheaper labour.
We wonder where our federal government is while this is happening to us. We wonder how a government can boast of a relocation program that sends 50 jobs to Newfoundland, ignores what has happened there in the past two years of industrial lay-offs, and sends 1,500 jobs to Sherbrooke, Quebec. We are not even sure they are going to get there, because of Bill 101. We wonder about these things. That is why I say you cannot put a price tag on confederation. But I can say this, and I say it with certainty: this union will not survive unless each province is given the right to fully develop its own potential within confederation. That, sir, is being denied to us by policies pursued by this government.
I do not resent the billions of dollars that are used to develop the tarsands of Alberta. I could say that in 1932, were it not for the government of Canada, Alberta would have gone under as a bankrupt province. Today, of course, it is hard to concede that rich Alberta was once in a state of bankruptcy and would have gone bankrupt where it not for the Government of Canada-the same situation that happened in my part of the world. Yet they have been allowed the tax incentives, through a world shortage of oil, to develop the potential of fossil fuels which are there and you have the situation in Alberta that you have today.
If we were to have only a small portion of what is going into the development of the Alberta tarsands to develop the vast potential of the lower Churchill River to provide transmission lines in order to get that undeveloped hydroelectric power into energy-hungry Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-and, indeed, part of Ontario, not to mention the potential that exists in the upper New York state-surely that would make just as much sense. Sir, it would make a great deal more sense,
(Mr. McGrath.]
because we have a renewable resource in hydroelectric energy as opposed to a definite resource with which we are dealing in the case of Alberta and the tarsands when we are talking about carbon or fossil fuels.
We wonder about these things, and we wonder how we could have arrived at a point in time when we have a government in this country that is conditioned-and, indeed, would condition the people of Canada-to accept as a fact of life an unemployment rate in one of its provinces that exceeds 27 per cent. This is an unprecedented situation in the history of our province. Long-term unemployment is disastrous in terms of its social consequences. It is disastrous in terms of its potential for unrest and, indeed, it is serving as a catalyst for our people to question whether or not we can afford to continue with the Prime Minister's brand of federalism.
Sir, it is not only Quebec that has a grievance with this government and its brand of federalism. We have only been in this union for 28 years. We brought into it these vast resources. Without us, the 200-mile limit off eastern Canada would be nothing, because 70 per cent of it was in the territorial waters of the Dominion of Newfoundland prior to 1949. We brought with us the rights to the offshore mineral resources because we had sovereignty in 1949.
Again that fact is being questioned by this government. It is a fact which ultimately the courts will have to decide. A country cannot continue with that kind of confrontation politics. A country which allows one of its parts which has great potential and great promise to go underdeveloped, without providing for tax incentives and the investment capital that is so essential to realize the maximum yields from this potentially wealthy province, cannot continue. My time is up, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to intervene until later in this debate, but I am prompted by the tremendous speech which has just been made by the hon. member for St. John's East to say a few words at this time and to support the plea he has made.
I represent a portion of the city of Winnipeg. I come from western Canada, where Newfoundland is a couple thousand miles away, but I want to devote these few words exclusively to support the plea that all parts of this country-and 1 think Newfoundland is the place to start-should share equally in the bounty and the possibilities of life in Canada.
In my view, the hon. member who has just resumed his seat has been talking about one of the most important issues which face this country. As he was speaking, I recalled an occasion quite a few years ago when I happened to be with M. J. Coldwell in the presence of Louis St. Laurent, who was commenting on what he had learned from a trip he had just made across Canada from coast to coast. It was in the early years of Mr. St. Laurent's prime ministership, and in those days, of course, trips from coast to coast were made by train.
November 25, 1977

I remember very well sitting in that small company and hearing the then prime minister say to the rest of us, "We have a great country. It is a wonderful Canada. But we will fail unless we get rid of the terrible regional inequalities." I happen to feel the same way about inequalities among individuals. I have spent most of my time in the years I have been here trying to correct those inequalities by pursuing social security measures, but parallel with that is the absolute necessity of getting over the notion expressed yesterday by the Prime Minister, and again today by the Minister of Finance, that we just have to take it for granted that some parts of the country are better off than others and that some have more natural resources than others.
The Prime Minister says that is what confederation is all about, the rich and the poor somehow getting along together. 1 think Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent was right when he said 25 years or more ago that we would have to do something about the regional inequalities in this country or Canada would not hold together.
Therefore, I want to give the endorsation of my voice, as that of a westerner, to the plea which has been made for a much better approach to the problems In Newfoundland than was demonstrated there yesterday by the Prime Minister and today by the Minister of Finance.
These issues are serious. National unity is an important issue, but it is not just between the rest of Canada and the province of Quebec. It is not over just language and those issues. It is primarily over economic issues. If we go on accepting, as a matter of course and as a matter of what we have to live with, forever these gross inequalities, the country will not be the one of which we could be so proud.
So I join with the previous speaker in calling for those policies in terms of taxation, employment, regional concerns and distribution of wealth which would give Canadians in all parts of Canada an equal opportunity. I congratulate the hon. member for St. John's East for the speech he has just made.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, I have a few more questions for the minister. I hope he is still with us somewhere. I come back to the line of questioning I was pursuing earlier. In answer to one of my questions, the minister made the point that there is an accrual, prices go up and the tax is on the capital gain portion of whatever the person has first of all bought and then sold.
I want to take the minister up on that comment. I wonder if he can indicate to what extent the imposition of the capital gains tax has, in itself, been inflationary. I am referring to the fact that people are now holding capital items-let us say a piece of real estate-and one of the things which is calculated is what the capital gains tax is gong to be if they sell. They automatically increase the price in anticipation of what they feel is a fair net to themselves, and the net result is that the tax revenue we are referring to as being something the federal government is very appreciative of is really being added to the value of real estate when it is sold, which in turn increases
Income Tax Act
tremendously the inflation factor which we have experienced as far as real estate is concerned. Can the minister indicate to what extent any of his department's work has substantiated what I am saying?

I do not agree at all with the hon. member, because in a market economy the market decides. If a person values his land higher because he anticipates some capital gains tax, the market will not bear that just for the sake of that. If we were to accept the argument of the hon. member, we would not have any capital gains tax at all-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I don't think he said that.

-because if the capital gains tax causes inflation, we would not have any capital gains tax. We have decided to have a capital gains tax. 1 heard the hon. member for Calgary North arguing against it a few minutes ago. It is strange that we have not always had a capital gains tax in Canada, because if we want to have a fair tax system we must tax all kinds of gains and not exempt some aspects. I do not share the view of the hon. member that the capital gains tax is a cause of inflation. It is a contribution from citizens who make gains to the service programs we have at this time.
The hon. member could make the same argument about any tax. He could argue that because any tax is a tax, it is inflationary. I think taxation is a system of redistribution of income, and taxes have to come from capital gains just as taxes come from personal gains.

Mr. Chairman, may I just follow on what the minister is saying? Frankly, I am rather disturbed to hear his emphasis about revenue because, as I think we are going to bring out fairly clearly later, in terms of the nearly $50 billion of spending the minister is probably going to ask us to accept for fiscal 1979, the total amount of revenue the government gets from the capital gains tax is comparatively small.
However, the main point I want to readdress to the minister is that while the marketplace operates, there have to be buyers and sellers, and sellers today take as one of their considerations the fact that they have to pay a capital gains tax, before they fix prices for their properties. The net result, based on the figure the minister gave us of about $255 million in capital gains tax revenue both at the federal and provincial level, is that that probably means the price of property has been moved up $500 million to $600 million by sellers in anticipation of paying a tax.
I hope it is not lost on the minister that in many instances it is not, in truth, a gain that has been realized. In constant dollars, the so-called gain in the eyes of the federal tax man is simply inflation. I gave the example of someone making a $10,000 investment which is sold for $10,880 after 12 months. In constant dollars, nothing has been gained, yet the investor will be taxed on $440 at whatever his going rate is. This has contributed to inflation in real estate in that prior to selling, people adjust for the tax and ask a higher price. The govern-

ment has put them in the position where if they hold on to the property, in effect they have a tax shelter. The tax is not levied until the property is disposed of, so it can be allowed to accrue.
Whereas an owner at one time would have been quite ready to sell, now he will not be as willing to sell quickly because of the federal or provincial capital gains tax he is liable for-and that, in effect, is confiscation of his property. Does the minister not realize what I have said?

Mr. Chairman, as I explained this morning, the capital gains tax is half the rate of normal taxes. The NDP said that the logical thing would have been to impose a 100 per cent tax, but we went for a 50 per cent tax. Now I understand the Tories advocate a policy of no capital gains tax at all. The hon. member said that next year the federal government will need perhaps $50 billion, and that capital gains is inflationary, at the same time arguing it is a very small amount of money, only $250 million. How can he claim that $250 million, out of a budget of $50 billion, puts great pressure on inflation?
There is no capital gains tax on homes. Does the hon. member argue that there has not been inflation in house property because the capital gains tax did not apply to home ownership? I do not understand his argument. When he says that a capital gain is not directly indexed, I should like to reply that it is taxed at half the rate of the income tax, and exemptions apply, so in fact there is a kind of indexation for capital gains because it is added to the revenue and taxed at half level after the deductions, which are increased every year according to inflation. We should not have double indexation for that income.

Mr. Chairman, I have been attempting to have a meaningful dialogue with the minister about something that is of great concern to many Canadians, and that is the impact of capital gains tax. This is one of the first opportunities we have had to review the actual figures and to review the rhetoric advanced at the time the capital gains tax was introduced into this House. I wish the minister were less partisan when he feels he is under pressure. I am simply trying to get his view about some of the aspects of capital gains that Canadians are concerned about.
I have never suggested that there should be a capital gains tax on a personal home. I am saying that where there is a capital gains tax, it has had an adverse effect and that people who are considering selling their homes decide to either hold them because of the tax shelter or they bounce the price to a level that will cover the tax which the federal and provincial treasuries will collect. I take it the minister does not have a great deal of concern for that inflationary impact, be it small or large. I simply say that as we reassess the capital gains tax, surely we should at least consider that type of thing.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to have too long a dialogue on that. I should like to point out to the House, however, that if you compare the inflation rates in Canada and in the United States, in the long run, generally speaking, it is the same. The United States has had a capital gains tax since
[Mr. Stevens.)
1913, however, and it does not seem to have impaired their development over the last 64 years. One can argue there is an element of that which could cause a little bit of inflation, and that argument could be made for every tax.
Of course, if there were not to be any tax anywhere, there would perhaps be less inflation. If there is to be no tax at all, of course, then the consequence would be that we would go back to "les cavernes", and I am not ready to go that far back.

Mr. Chairman, I find it interesting, the way the minister likes to use figures from the United States when it suits his purpose. He is not so quick to use the inflation figures of the United States in the question period when we point out to him that the current inflation rate there, on an annual basis, was 3.8 per cent in the last three months, compared to 8.8 per cent in this country.
The minister made reference to the point made by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge which I think he took rather out of context. As I understand what our colleague was saying, it was to the effect that there may be more equity instead of this so-called rough justice plan of saying only half the gain will be taken for tax purposes. As I understood the hon. member, he was saying it might be a more equitable approach to say that capital gains would be fully indexed; that the entire capital gain would be taken after indexing. In that sense, the confiscation I spoke of could be avoided where there may be a gain in current dollars, but in constant dollars it is no gain at all. Did the minister fully understand the contrast made by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge?

Mr. Chairman, I will take note of that, but the implications are quite serious. If we carry the hon. member's logic to its conclusion, it means we should have 100 per cent capital gains and indexing just as we do with other incomes. In order to achieve that, we would have to raise the taxes on capital gains to 100 per cent and consider the gain just as ordinary income. From there, the system of indexing would apply. I hope the business community in Toronto will react to the suggestion of the hon. member for York-Simcoe.

Mr. Chairman, I will let the record speak for itself, but clearly I was not saying what the minister is trying to put into my mouth. It may be of some help to the minister to say that I hope there is no doubt in his mind, or that of any other member, that this party believes capital gains should be indexed before they are taxed. That is our firm policy and we do not have any hesitation in advancing it. We wish the government would accept that type of proposal without fudging the issue.
If I could go back to my questioning before lunch at which time I was interested in the tax revenue received in 1975 with respect to capital gains, both at the federal and the provincial level, perhaps the minister could give us some breakdown as to the over-all capital gain which has been experienced, also the capital losses-in short, a fairly clear picture of what in fact was the experience with regard to capital gains in 1975.

Of course, I have always been inclined to side with the Liberals rather than with the Progressive Conservatives.

Mr. Chairman, if we can come back to clause 1 of Bill C-ll, it deals with this question of capital gains. Up until now persons could only claim $1,000 from capital gains loss against their income. Maybe, in the future, if clause 1 goes through, they will be able to claim $2,000 against their income. It is to that I would like to address my further comments, if I may.
We were dealing specifically with the question of what has been the impact of capital gains as far as tax revenue is concerned and, second, to what extent losses have been net-table against taxable gains. My question to the minister, you will recall, Mr. Chairman, was very simple. When we have the over-all gross figures, we find that the capital losses were $409 million against capital gains of $1,065 million. However, when we find the taxable losses, the losses, while not insignificant, are quite small in the sense that they fall from $409 million in the gross figure to only $71 million, whereas the capital gains that are taxable remain relatively high.
I will accept the minister's word that this is fairly technical to describe why there should be a relatively small loss which is chargeable against your taxable gains. However, I ask the minister if he agrees that this is further evidence of a certain inequity that presently exists in our capital gains process. It is one thing to tax the man who has the gain, but surely it should work that the losses that people are incurring are also to be quite readily chargeable against those gains.
On reflection, I wonder if the minister has any further suggestion as to why there seems to be this sharp fall off from the gross figures compared to the taxable figures with regard to tax losses.

Mr. Chairman, I think we can argue over this for a long time. Perhaps I can give the committee an explanation. We have, of course, received a number of representations on this. These representations have suggested that there should be no limit on the deductibility of capital losses. This will not only be costly in terms of revenue, but will permit the reduction of taxes by many taxpayers with a significant investment portfolio, those we call the rich.
Taxpayers could arrange to dispose of those securities on which losses are accrued in order to realize the losses and hold on to those securities which have increased in value. In these circumstances taxable income should be reduced by losses even if the accrued gain exceeds the loss. Therefore if there were no limit on this allowance for capital losses, only those losses in
[The Chairman.]
excess of accrued gains should be deducted. It is a question of tax.

It is necessary, Mr. Chairman, in a system such as ours to tax at a given time the income of all people, even their capital gains. It is a logical thing; otherwise, part of the population would actually be fully exempted from their social obligations as taxpayers, while their taxes allow us, to set up programs designed to effect equalization payments to the poorer provinces, payments which substantially help Newfoundland, for example, or Quebec or New Brunswick, and go to pay old age pensions and so on.
Should we exempt richer people from taxation because they claim that their losses in a specific year are greater than they would wish? Such is the market system and the capitalist system. One must either win or lose. If we were to allow tax deductions every year for losses incurred, I am sure that a great many rich people in this country would use this system to hide a lot of revenues and avoid paying taxes as ordinary people like us pay year in and year out. Therefore rich and poor Canadian alike must put part of their revenues at the service of their fellow citizens through a taxation system. This $2,000 exemption is providing an incentive to take risks but if somebody has taken such risks incurring great losses, it is because he took too many risks and he must therefore pay the consequences. That is why other revenues should not be tax exempt.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has led me exactly into the next line of questioning that 1 want to put to him. He left the impression that somehow this is a tax of the wealthy. That is clearly a misunderstanding on the government side. It is perhaps why the hon. member for York-Scarborough was so anxious in the sense that his point was that he felt it was a tax on the poor. In that sense perhaps he has a much greater point than I had realized.
I direct the minister's attention to the final column of the tax statistics to which I have referred. He will notice that approximately 40 per cent of the capital gains is earned by those with earnings of less than $20,000. Quite a large portion of the gain we are considering here, and out of which they make their revenue, is not from the so-called fat cats but from the average hard working Canadians who are earning something below $20,000.
If you go into the next category, $20,000 to $25,000, you find another 10 per cent. If you go to the $25,000 income level, approximately 50 per cent of the total gain on people who are paying capital gains tax is paid by people who are earning less than $25,000 a year. Forty per cent is paid by those earning under $20,000.
I would like to put this further question to the minister. Is he aware of this? Does he agree that this is a tax that quite significantly falls on relatively low income people in this country?

Mr. Chairman, that is exactly the point we are making by increasing this to $2,000. I am told that, generally speaking, those earning less than $20,000 do not derive a great part of their income from investment. We are doubling the exemption for the losses so that these people can benefit from this tax measure that we are proposing. Either we have or do not have an equitable tax system in this country. In order to have an equitable tax system, we decided that we had to do what the United States did in 1913, namely, to have a capital gains tax in Canada.
I remind the committee that, when we introduced the capital gains tax, we got rid of the old system of succession duties at the federal level. We did this because we wanted to permit people at time of death to pass on to their descendants in some easier fashion what they had accumulated in terms of wealth.

Mr. Chairman, may I come back to my basic point. With indexing there would really be less of an inequity, bearing in mind that indexing would benefit, to the extent of 50 per cent of those who make a gain, people who earn
Income Tax Act
$25,000 a year or less. The minister says this is why he is raising, to $2,000 instead of $1,000, the privilege to write off a loss against other income.
With all due respect, surely the minister is missing the point. This allows a person who has sustained a loss to write it off against other income, but there are very few people earning less than $20,000 a year who would welcome the prospect of writing off a $2,000 loss. My point is, what about the man who has not made a loss but a gain of the kind to which I have referred? While in terms of current dollars it appears to be a gain, because there is no indexing it is in fact a confiscation of his capital in the sense that he is being taxed on something which in constant dollars is in truth not a gain. It is not a question of allowing him to write off a loss. I am concerned about a person who has made a gain. Fifty per cent of the total gains that were made were made by people earning less than $25,000. What about that person?
Mr. Chairman, I should like to repeat what I have said many, many times, namely, that capital gains are taxed at half the rate of a person's normal income.
It is still confiscation.

All of an individual's exemptions are indexed. If the hon. member is arguing the we should go back to the time of the dinosaurs, that is one thing. I know he is against capital gains, and so is the hon. member for Calgary North. Generally speaking, members of the NDP want us to tax them at 100 per cent. Like any other income, a buck is a buck. But typically we Liberals find a good compromise between these two extremes which, although it satisfies neither of the two extremes, satisfies the great majority of the Canadian people because they keep voting for us from year to year.

Mr. Chairman, the minister makes reference to going back to the age of the dinosaurs. It was represented to this House that the capital gain which was going to be taxed was the gain from shares. How is it that it has now shifted to real estate? Sometimes, Mr. Chairman, I despair at the lack of knowledge in the Department of Finance. The parliamentary secretary stands up and says that somehow or other home prices are not being affected. market, not the share market which initially it was said would be the chief source of the capital gains tax?

In answer to the hon. member, I would simply like to say that of course we shall never be able to agree with the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) on this point. What can we do? The taxpayers, the workers have their taxes deducted from their pay cheque. They have no other choice. After many years we discovered that by speculating on the stock market some people could avoid contributing to the social needs of this country. We then decided to tax capital gains. The hon. member does not agree. As I was associated with the income tax reform, I remember very well that this was recommended. This is ironical since it was recommended by the Carter report, among others, and the Carter report was published by the Carter Commission. This commission was established by the Progressive Conservative government in 1961-62. The Conservatives are therefore refusing to recognize their offspring, but we are more human than that; we find it fair to tax capital gains. The most capitalistic of all countries, the United States, was taxing capital gains in 1913. I was not even born then. As a matter of fact, this was a long time before my birth.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say to the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Clermont) that it is very difficult in a society as complex as ours to give in to requests from all those who would like tax exemptions for something or other. There is only one clear problem, and I am not a Social Crediter like my friend from Roberval (Mr. Gauthier). I know that the money we spend is taken from the pockets of the taxpayers, and we try to be as fair as possible about it. And we, as well as everyone who has reflected for a moment on this matter, including the commission created by a Progressive Conservative government, the Carter Commission, have discovered that there should be a capital gains tax. Obviously I shall never be able to settle the issue of principle from which stem the diverging views of my friend from York-Simcoe and myself, but, Mr. Chairman, we are still on clause 1, which increases the loss exemption from $ 1,000 to $2,000 for capital gains.
Income Tax Act
There are 160 clauses to be studied in this committee. Since we have started the study of this clause at noontime, it has not progressed by an inch. It might be necessary to wait until Monday or Tuesday or even Wednesday before clause 1 which contains only three lines gets its approval. It is quite clear and it does not take a genius to understand that we are raising from $1,000 to $2,000 the tax exemption for people who claim capital losses. It is obvious that once again the opposition is trying to prolong the debate simply to delay the work of this House rather than passing this bill as soon as possible. There are thousands of decisions in the business community which cannot be taken at the present time. Given the attitude taken by the Progressive Conservatives, it may be that we will never succeed in passing this bill. However, we have been able to impose a time allocation on second reading, so I guess they want us to do the same thing at the committee stage. I have no objection to that. We might spend three or four days studying clause 1, then the other clauses will be studied much more rapidly.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance which relates to the statement made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe when he blamed the prices of housing in Ontario, and in Toronto in particular, on capital gains tax.
Would the hon. minister not agree the principal reason for the cost of housing in Toronto being higher than most parts of the country is because, even though the Government of Canada has had a law on its books since 1953 which allowed for federal funding of land acquisition and land banking, it was never used to any extent by the government of Ontario? Also, would he not agree that the government of Ontario land development policies have consistently favoured land speculation in the Toronto and Ottawa areas, the result of which has been that people have taken advantage of these federal grants that were, and are available, except for the last two or three years? This is the main reason for the cost of housing in Toronto being $20,000 more than other parts of the country. It has nothing to do with capital gains tax.

Mr. Chairman, capital gains tax on private residences does not exist because they are exempt. There has been a lot of land speculation. The hon. member for Laprairie blames it on the Ontario administration, but I do not want to comment too much about the provincial situation. Not long ago a very learned gentleman from Ontario, Walter Gordon, indicated in a speech that approximately 100 approvals are required to develop land in Ontario. Also he indicated that it requires many inquiries in order to do that. I do not know. I am not a resident of Ontario, so I cannot judge that. It is not due to capital gains at all.
Land speculation is not under federal jurisdiction. The permits for construction, the development of the land, and so on, are within provincial and municipal areas. To attempt to shift the burden on to capital gains is either stretching the argument a bit far, or the hon. member is simply stretching his
80027-12W

Income Tax Act
speech in an attempt to use up the remaining time until four o'clock, and thus clause 1 will not be passed.

Mr. Chairman, I have a brief question 1 want to put to the minister, and it is mostly for the record. Until recently an argument has been put forward against the capital gains tax that it was really a tax for equity purposes, and that in fact it was not much of a revenue producer, and even from the viewpoint of equity there were objections to it. The figures that the minister has produced for us today indicate that it is more than just an equity measure-we are talking about relatively big money which is now coming in from capital gains. Does the minister have some figures to indicate whether the take from the capital gains is increasing or holding its own? My own personal recollection is that, when it first came in, the income from capital gains was a relatively small amount of around $40 million. That seems to be increasing substantially as the years go by.

The income from the tax is now $255 million. That is a good sum of money. Of course as the hon. member knows very well, capital gains before 1972 were not taxable, only the gains since 1974. Of course the amount is increasing every year. I do not know exactly by how much it is increasing. I have the figures for 1975 but not for 1976. The essential increase was from 1974 to 1975. I do not have the actual figures with me but I will provide them for the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I noticed this afternoon that in his answer to a question he was asked, the minister said that at a given time people were saving too much. I would like him to give us something precise as to what he meant because we are all well aware of the campaigns made by several financial institutions to incite people to save more. So I would like the minister to be more precise on what he meant by his remarks that people are saving too much.

Mr. Chairman, at the present time there is an insufficient demand in our economy. During the past three years, the level of savings has been rather constant and maintained at a very high level. I believe that Canadians are setting aside about 10 per cent of their income for savings.
This is excellent if it lasts for a year, but when it goes on for three years in a row problems begin to arise. I am urging people who have been putting money away for the last two or three years to spend part of it on consumer goods, particularly Canadian goods, to revitalize our economy and create jobs. Because it is very difficult to ask industry to expand when capacity utilization is only 80 per cent.
Of course there are programs to promote savings. We will always need savings, but within limits. I urge those who have enough savings to realize how worthwhile it would be to spend at this point. This does not mean by any stretch of the imagination that nobody must save. But those who have too much should spend at this point, to help revitalize our Canadian economy. This is what I meant, because during the last
[Mr. Chr6tien.1
three years I understand the level of savings has been at least 100 per cent higher than during the three preceeding years. In the current economic context where consumer expenditures are lagging, it would help if people with a lot of savings started doing some spending, particularly if they toured Canada rather than going further down south. I for one will be doing so at Christmas time. I said so and I was embarrassed myself because I had planned to go down south, but I realized it is better for me as a citizen to remain here at Christmas time and go skiing instead of sunbathing. So, in view of our $2 billion deficit for this year on the tourist trade account alone, I hope this will be done and also that we buy Canadian goods as much as possible so that our Canadian production capacity utilization is increased.

You should have told the Prime Minister to do that.
Before I get into some more questioning on clause 1 I must respond, at least in part, to some of the comments made by the minister in his impassioned plea after he returned. I wish to assure the minister that no one in this Chamber took any exception to his leaving.
You did.

No. In fact we thought we were quite co-operative. I said that rather than having a delay I would put my questions to the parliamentary secretary, questions to which subsequently the parliamentary secretary, I thought, responded very effectively.

I am sorry, and I take the hon. members' word. Someone had told me the hon. member had given me hell because I was out of the Chamber. If he did not, then I withdraw what I said, but I cannot withdraw my need to get out.

Mr. Chairman, let me assure the minister that we realize he does have certain human sides.
There are other points on which perhaps I should comment. The minister has left the unfortunate impression that there has been an undue delay with regard to discussion of clause 1, and he referred to the fact that we had not even passed the title to the bill. As the minister knows, the title is one of the last things we pass, not one of the first. I would point out to the minister, who surely keeps the score, that there have been more people questioning him on clause 1 on the government side of the House then there have been members questioning him from this side. If he wants to put the usual governmental gag on his own followers, he had better talk to them.

Mr. Chairman, may I say that the hon. member, who had the floor for the third time now and used up 20 minutes, should recognize that members on my side are not as confused as hon. members opposite, so that they can put just one question and obtain satisfaction.
November 25, 1977

While I have the floor I would like to answer the question put by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge who asked me about the capital gains tax. There has been an increase since we introduced the capital gains tax. Taxable capital gains went up from $239 million in 1972 to $431 million in 1973, to $507 million in 1974, and $680 million in 1975. These are the capital gains reported; the tax on them is less because people pay only half the normal rate on them.

I must assure the minister that if he keeps interrupting me, naturally time will keep running. I have a few questions I want to put to him, and surely the more he becomes impassioned and makes these various comments, the more he makes it impossible for me to do anything but correct the record.
What I was saying on clause 1 was that I feel it is pertinent to know that more questions have been directed to him from his own followers than there have been from this side. As the minister knows, clause 1 is generally the clause on which people make general comments on the bill. Comments on this clause are not solely restricted to a specific item.
Let us not forget that the minister left the impression that once the capital gains tax was written in stone into the law of the land there should be no question on it thereafter. Such are not the facts. What I have tried to make clear is that when we introduced the capital gains tax certain recommendations were made, and this is virtually the first opportunity we have had in the House to review the impact of the capital gains tax and to ask the Minister of Finance whether he feels that certain aspects of what has transpired are in truth equitable. One of those is our suggestion that there should be indexing of the capital gains tax rather than the so-called rough justice formula whereby we only take in half of the gain.
I do not think members of the House should be too impatient, because we must bear in mind that it was on this side of the House that the suggestion was first advocated for the indexing of the income tax. It took the government many years finally to catch on to what we were talking about and to realize that there was an inequity. Perhaps in the faint hope that it might win some votes the government said, "Fine, we are going to bring in indexing," because it realized that was an equitable thing and possibly even popular. Is there anything wrong with our at least exploring the possibility that indexing would also be a relevant thing for capital gains?
There was another reference made by one of the minister's colleagues to the fact that I referred to land prices going up in value, and that perhaps one of the things which had contributed to those prices going up was the fact that many speculators who are in the land development business have been using the system in a way they felt would at least compensate them for the tax they have had to pay with regard to capital gains. Somehow my simple pointing out that home prices in Canada are about one third higher than they are in the United States got twisted by the minister's colleague into some representation about Toronto prices.
Income Tax Act
I never referred to Toronto prices. The hon. member somehow wanted to twist it so that somehow it was the fault of the Ontario government after all. I am talking about prices from Nova Scotia right through to Victoria.
Newfoundland.

All right, St. John's. I hope the record is clear on that.
Let me put a different question now to the minister concerning capital gains. We have explored the impact, the revenue, who is actually paying and the fact that indexing is apparently not under any serious consideration as far as the department is concerned.
There is a second injustice with regard to capital gains. A person has the option either to liquidate every year and pay the tax payable at whatever his tax rate is for that year or, as many people are doing, bunching or holding their capital realization until a later time rather than paying the tax. Where the inequity comes in is when the person finally does sell his property.
Let us take my example of $10,000. Let us say that a person says he does not want to liquidate at possibly $10,800 because he just does not want to have to pay that tax. Let us say he holds it ten years. At the rate of inflation under this government it will probably be that he will have to sell that property for $20,000 in order to get the same buying power he could get last year with his $10,000. Under the present set-up-and I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong-the only thing this person can then do in 1986 would be to take his $20,000 and put it into some type of annuity for up to 15 years if he wants to dollar average the gain. In short, there is no provision allowing him to have a charge-back, say, for the previous ten years of $1,000 per year and to come into the lower tax bracket. The fact is he will have to pay whatever his tax rate is in the year 1986 on the whole $10,000 falling into his income that year and, as I have said, a high portion of that or, in my example all of it, will simply be an inflationary gain.
Is the minister aware of that bunching inequity which is occurring, and is there any consideration being given to relieving that situation?

Mr. Chairman, we are aware of that problem as well as of many other problems, including indexing in relation to capital gain. The provisions are not written in stone, as the hon. member said. We are constantly reviewing the tax system in every budget. We have a bill containing 160 clauses before the House at this time. We review the tax system every year, or every six months depending upon whether we are having two budgets in a year. The arguments of the hon. member will be looked into by the experts of my department, and we will see if we have to bring about some changes in the next budget.

Realizing that there are rather technical and somewhat complicated aspects to the whole capital gains tax situation I wonder if the minister would indicate if he would be

November 25, 1977
Income Tax Act
willing to make a special reference of this subject to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs so that there can be an in depth appraisal carried out as to the success or failure of the capital gains tax system, so that indexing can be reviewed and so that we could perhaps call witnesses and receive briefs on what people now feel about it. Frankly, I feel that the minister is sincere, and I have no reason to doubt that.
The whole tax system is an ongoing and very volatile thing. It would be quite constructive between now and the time he brings in a budget to have the benefit of a committee review of the whole question of the capital gains tax in this country. My next question will come later.

Mr. Chairman, I am considering referring problems to the committee, but I have not decided to go along with this as yet. I will take into consideration the request of the hon. member, but I did not have such a thing in mind.

My next question comes from a suggestion which was made as long ago as perhaps 1971 by the hon. member for Edmonton West. I felt he suggested a rather innovative approach, that as far as Canadians are concerned- and the hon. member restricted it to the question of investing in the resource industry; I perhaps might want to expand on that to include any Canadian investment, be it resource or manufacturing-there should be a formula worked out with regard to capital gains which would make them non-taxable depending on the number of years an investment is held. For example, I think the hon. member's thinking was that if an investment were held for five years, there would be no taxable gain on the basis that that is obviously a relatively long-term investment and should not be taxed as current income. However, for every year short of that, the suggestion was that a person should lose 20 per cent of his total 100 per cent non-taxable position, and if he bought and sold something within a year it would be fully taxable. Has any thought been given to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton West?
We are aware of that suggestion. It has been looked into, but it has not been recommended to the minister.

HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AND CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO SHORTEN PERIOD WITHIN WHICH BY-ELECTIONS MUST BE CALLED
speechtext:
that Bill C-211, to amend the House of Commons Act and the Canada Elections Act (by-elections), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I hope, rather than talking this bill out today, that the subject matter will be allowed to go to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections so that this House can deal with the very important principle involved. At the committee any necessary amendments to lengthen or shorten the time period proposed in the bill could be made.
I should like to open the debate by saying the importance of the bill is underscored by the fact that there are now five seats in this House vacant, thus effectively denying representation to over 680,000 Canadians. Under our present laws which govern the holding of by-elections this is a situation which is unlikely to be soon corrected. It is not a new issue, however. Every government in the history of the country, whether Progressive Conservative of Liberal, has abused the present laws on byelections to ensure they are held only at what is considered the most politically expedient moment. It is a record of which none of those governments or we as Canadians can be proud.
Quite apart from the intolerable situation where Canadians are denied a voice in government through their elected representatives, the issues surrounding any delay in the holding of a
November 25, 1977

by-election reflect some very old and very basic concepts essential to our system of democratic government.
Any such delay openly flouts our belief in the importance of the participation of all Canadians in our political process. In the past ten years we have heard much of participatory democracy. It seems to me that the representation of all Canadians in this House should be the cornerstone of participatory democracy. It should also be restated here that a central issue to the development of our parliamentary institutions and traditions was the idea of "no taxation without representation". Over a period of hundreds of years thousands of people have gone to war, fought, died, in order to gain the right of elected representation. This is a principle which has been fought for long and hard.
Today we have in Canada "taxation without representation". Those people in the five constituencies of Burnaby-Rich-mond-Delta in British Columbia, Hamilton-Wentworth in Ontario, York-Scarborough in Ontario, Fundy-Royal in New Brunswick, and Lotbiniere in Quebec, still pay taxes, yet have no elected representation. This bill also reflects a debate that has been going on in Canada for the past ten years-the role and importance of this House and of individual members in our political process.
I would suggest that a situation which allows unnecessary delays in filling a seat vacated through the death or resignation of a member is an insult to each and every member in this House, for it suggests that it is not important that some Canadians are not represented for unduly extended periods of time. It suggests that it is not important that all Canadians have a voice in this House of Commons. It suggests that an elected representative is not essential either to the people of a constituency or to the governing of this country. Worst of all it is a situation that suggests that political expediency take precedence over all other principles.
In Canada, under our present law, upon the death or resignation of a member, a writ for a by-election does not have to be issued until six months-approximately 180 days-after the Speaker is informed of the vacancy. At the end of that six months there is presently no provision that states a by-election must be called within a specific time frame. After the six months the writ could then be issued, setting the by-election date one month away, one year away, or even two or three years away.
I put forward this bill because quite simply the present situation is wrong. The present situation flouts the basic democratic principle of entitlement to elected representation. This bill would redress the situation by reducing the six months' period for the issuing of the writ to 60 days, and would require a by-election date to be set within 60 days after the writ is issued. This bill allows for a maximum total lapse of time, from when the Speaker is notified of a vacancy and the polling date, of 120 days.
I said before that our present law suggests that political expediency takes precedence. To verify that look at page 11,619 in Hansard of March 9, 1976. We have seen, quite recently, expediency at work. When the Hon. Gerard Pelletier
By-Elections
resigned his seat to become Canada's ambassador to France, the government was able to bring about a by-election within 41 days. At the same time as Mr. Pelletier resigned, Walter Carter, the member for St. John's West, also resigned. The by-election in St. John's West took place 13 months-that is, one year and one month or over 390 days-after Mr. Carter's resignation. The situation in St. John's West was the longest vacancy in the 110-year history of our parliament. That was, incidentally, also at a time when the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada was appearing before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, making recommendations to shorten substantially the time of national election campaigns.
Let us consider other countries. How do we compare? I am afraid not very favourably.
The problem of filling vacated seats is not unique to Canada, but is common to all western democracies, and I would like now to outline how other democracies deal with it. In western European countries members are often not elected on a constituency basis, but on the basis of their position on lists of candidates provided by their political parties and the apportioning of seats according to the percentage of the popular vote their party receives in a general election. This is commonly referred to as proportional representation. As such, these countries do not have by-elections, but they do recognize the importance of filling every seat after a vacancy occurs, and have instituted mechanisms to achieve this.
In the Netherlands, for example, the political party concerned simply fills the seat with the first name appearing on the party list remaining from the previous election, effective immediately. There is no time delay here in filling a vacancy. In other countries, such as Sweden, every member has an alternate who immediately takes the seat should it be vacated.
In the United States, on the death or resignation of a senator or congressman, the governor of the affected state is empowered to appoint a replacement immediately. The U.S. system clearly recognizes, even though members of the House of Representatives face an election every two years, that full representation in the Congress is needed at all times.
In the United Kingdom, under the provisions of the Representation of the Peoples Act, 1948 and 1969, upon notice of a vacancy the Speaker issues a warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, who forthwith issues a writ for a by-election. Nomination papers must then be delivered no earlier than the fourth day, and no later than the ninth day after the writ is issued in the case of a county constituency; in the case of a borough or urban constituency no earlier than the third day, and no later than the seventh day after the writ is issued. The returning officer of the constituency then fixes a polling day no earlier than the seventh day, nor later than the ninth day after the last day for delivery of nomination papers. The minimum time before the holding of a by-election in the United Kingdom is, therefore, ten days after the Speaker has been notified; the absolute maximum is 18 days after issuance of the writ. There are no politically expedient delays in England. In the United

November 25, 1977
By-Elections
Kingdom they recognize the democratic principle of filling a vacated seat with an elected representative quickly.
In Australia, under the Commonwealth Electoral Act of 1918 and 1973, section 33 of the act compels the Speaker to issue a writ for a by-election upon receiving notice of a vacancy. Nomination papers must then be filed no later than 21 days and no earlier than 7 days after the writ is issued according to section 62(10). Under section 63, a polling date is set no less than seven days and no more than 30 days after the last date for nomination. In Australia, therefore, the minimum time between the notification of a Speaker, the issuance of the writ and the holding of a by-election is 14 days. The absolute maximum is 51 days.
In New Zealand, under the New Zealand Electoral Act of 1956, and under Section 72(2) of that act, the Speaker as soon as he knows of the vacancy must immediately publish a notice in the Gazette and direct a warrant to the clerk of writs to issue a writ to fill the vacancy. Under section 74 the clerk then issues a writ no later than 21 days after receipt of the warrant or, in exceptional cases and only if an Order-in-Council requests postponement, the clerk issues a writ no later than 42 days after receipt of the warrant. Under section 76 of the New Zealand legislation, a by-election must be held within 50 days after issuance of the writ. In New Zealand the absolute maximum time between the Speaker being notified of a vacancy, the issuance of his warrant and the holding of a by-election is 92 days. The usual practice in New Zealand is only 71 days.
The countries of western Europe, where proportional representation is common, fill their vacancies automatically- in a matter of days after the vacancy has been created.
In comparison then to the three Commonwealth countries- Britain, Australia, and New Zealand, the maximum time lapse between when the Speaker is notified of a vacant seat and the holding of a by-election, is 92 days. Compare this to the appalling 13 months, or, if you like, one year and one month and in the case of the St. John's West by-election here in Canda it was over 390 days. However, legally in Canada it could be two or three years after the vacancy before a by-election is held. We should be ashamed of ourselves in this country.
Under this bill, which I propose today, Mr. Speaker, a maximum time lapse between notice of a vancancy and the holding of a by-election is 120 days, more than any other western democratic country. And yet this would surely give us more than enough time.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, there are presently five vacant seats in this House from four provinces, with a combined population of over 680,000 people. One of these seats, York-Scarborough, is by population the second largest constituency in Canada with over 248,000 constituents. On March 8th, 1976, as reported at page 11,572 of Hansard I asked our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the reason for the delay in calling a by-election in St. John's West. At that time he reaffirmed that he and the government believed that one of the fundamental rights in our democratic society is the right of a properly accredited electorate in any constituency in Canada
[Mr. Dick.)
to representation by elected officials in the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker, I believe that all members on all sides of this House share that belief. I would ask them, then, to reaffirm that belief by allowing this bill to go to committee, by assisting in the passage of this bill for the sake of the over
680,000	Canadians who are presently not represented in this House, and for the sake of the high principles upon which our democratic system is based. We have a duty to make sure that we retain full representation in this House of Commons as much as possible. We must correct that which is wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AND CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO SHORTEN PERIOD WITHIN WHICH BY-ELECTIONS MUST BE CALLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by commending the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton on the obvious concern he shows toward adequate representation, and for the constituents who, as a result of resignation or death of a member, find themselves without one. The fact that this bill is before us today is perhaps an indication of how strongly members feel about the administration of the Elections Act in general. Bill C-5, which is now before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, was the product of a great deal of consultation, but it has not included the amendment which the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) would like to see, and it does not include a number of amendments which I would like to see. This too is maybe an indication of the difficulty in reaching agreement as to the best way in which to achieve the end we all feel so strongly about.
Bill C-5, that cluster of amendments to the Canada Elections Act which is now before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, has three groups of amendments.
The first group came out of a working group which originally met on election expenses but as a result of their work brought forward some concerns about other parts of the act. That working group had representation on it from the four registered political parties in the House of Commons. There were three members from each party which made up the group that worked with the Chief Electoral Officer for about three years. Even at the end of all that extensive study they have not brought in amendments that meet the views of all of us.
The particular amendment before us in Bill C-211 would present some difficulties. I am not suggesting these difficulties are insuperable, but I suggest they need to be addressed, whether in committee or elsewhere. Section 6(1) and Section 10 of the House of Commons Act require the Speaker to address his warrant concerning a vacancy to the Chief Electoral Officer "forthwith". Subsection 13(1) of the House of Commons Act requires that a writ shall be issued within six months after the receipt by the Chief Electoral Officer of the warrant.
Section 22(1) of the Canada Elections Act requires that the governor in council shall fix the day upon which the poll shall be held at an election. The effect of this is that while the writ of election at a by-election must be issued within six months of the vacancy occurring in the House, the governor in council
November 25, 1977

can set polling day in the writ for any day subsequent to the six months. There is, in effect, no fixed time within which a by-election must be called except with regard to the dissolution of parliament or the expiration of the maximum five year term of parliament.
The bill before us would stipulate a maximum period of 120 days from the occurrence of the vacancy until polling day. The hon. member who presented the bill has certainly amassed a very impressive array of precedents as used in other countries. As I listened to him, however, I thought of our particular geography and our climatic conditions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could complete my remarks and then accept questions at the end. The by-election writs are only superseded and withdrawn where parliament is dissolved after the issuance of the new by-election writ. There are obvious complications one could see resulting from that. I am sorry the hon. member becomes so angry at having his ideas questioned because I am not opposed to the principle of the bill, and I was hoping that some of these matters could be addressed in committee or on a further occasion. Also, I said at the beginning that while I see these difficulties, I am not suggesting they are insuperable.
The cost of by-elections is something that has to be taken into consideration because they are extremely expensive. If the bill before us were accepted and we were locked into a fixed time with no flexibility or options, and if we had a by-election followed almost immediately by a general election, one would have to consider very carefully the effect of this.
The cost of a by-election will vary from constituency to constituency. However, according to the figures given by the Chief Electoral Officer in committee last week, the recent general election cost $29V2 million, of which $10'/2 million went into enumeration. About $4'/2 million went into printing the lists. Obviously that was a general election where there
By-Elections
may well have been some economies of scale. I expect a by-election figure would be proportionately more expensive.
The recent amendments to the Election Expenses Act added payment of some of the candidates' expenses. This is an additional expense factor which needs to be taken into consideration. The hon. member's point about the need for constituencies to be consistently represented is very valid. However, the total lack of flexibility in this bill concerns me.
The other question that I have is the idea of referring to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections amendments to the Canada Elections Act on a piecemeal basis. Bill C-5 which is now before the standing committee is based in part on the recommendations which came from the all-party working committee that worked for three years, primarily on election expenses, as well as other aspects of the act. Also included in the present Bill C-5 are some of the recommendations which the Chief Electoral Officer made and which were studied by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections last year. There is also the subject matter of three private members' bills.
Even with this amount of co-ordination, we still have a bill which does not meet everybody's requirements. I am not sure that the way to solve this problem is by adding yet another bill to deal with one specific aspect. I suggest there is more work to be done in committee by amending Bill C-5 and by enlarging it before we can proceed to further amendments to the Canada Elections Act.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to indicate very strong support of the bill that has been introduced by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick). I hope that the portions of the speech just made by my friend, the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), which indicated support will be the portions that will be implemented rather than her concern about certain difficulties.
It is interesting the number of myths and practices that have grown up around this business of the holding of by-elections. I recall not many weeks ago, when His Honour the Speaker announced the issuing of certain writs, my friend, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), asking me why it was that the writ had not yet been issued for the constituency formerly represented by the late Andre Fortin. I explained to him that although we had spent time on the floor of the House expressing regret at the loss of our colleague, and although Mr. Speaker had sent our expressions of sympathy to the widow and the family, Mr. Speaker still had not been officially notified, so nothing had been done. Therefore my hon. friends had to give the official notice so that that writ could be issued.
A number of other events have occurred in my memory. Reference has been made to the fact that although the government must set the date and must do the setting within six months after the notice has been given by the Speaker, the actual date can be put off indefinitely. I remember in particu-

November 25, 1977
By-Elections
lar, in the parliament of 1940 to 1945, that as we got close to the end of that parliament there was at least one vacancy, the seat of Kenora-Rainy River, and in fact there may have been two. The setting of the date for that election or for the two of them was put off until finally, when the six months had expired, Mr. King announced that the date had been set; but of course the date was in August or September of 1945, and everybody knew that because of the lapse of five years there would have to be a general election not later than June. So there has been a lot of fun playing around with this question.
I was also interested, if I may be pardoned for a personal reference, in the remarks just made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services (Miss Nicholson) to the effect that a four month limit such as suggested by my hon. friend could throw a by-election into the middle of winter. In my own case my predecessor, the late J. S. Woodsworth, died on March 21, 1942. The by-election could easily have been held that summer or fall, but it was delayed until November 30, which in Winnipeg is in the middle of winter. So as I say, Mr. Speaker, there has been a lot of manoeuvring with respect to this matter.
I believe the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton is right in asking that we lay down some specific rules such as are suggested in his bill. As he has just pointed out, there could be a change; the period could be lengthened or shortened, or we could provide that the rule not apply if a parliament had been in existence, say, for four and a half years. But in general I think that this idea should be adopted. The right of a government to be able to play around with this kind of thing and hold by-elections off to suit its convenience is totally inconsistent, I think with the democratic process.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services expressed a view that we often hear from that side, that she does not like things like this being dealt with on a piecemeal basis. Well, Mr. Speaker, there are two sides to that argument. If you go one way, you get one side; if you go the other way, you get the other. If a private member brings in a bill with three or four proposals in it, the answer is, "There is too much there; if there were only one point we could deal with it". But if you bring in only one proposition, it is said it is piecemeal. It seems to me that the crucial and important point here is the right of our people to be represented in the parliament of the day, and so I think that the principle of this bill deserves support.
If it is not possible for the bill as such to be given second reading and sent to standing committee, I hope that at five o'clock there will at least be agreement to send its subject matter, for it is one that is very important.

One of the things which I think we forget is how deeply the people feel about not being represented. As I walked from door to door in the constituency of Ottawa-Carleton that wonderful summer, the capital punishment bill had only recently gone through the House and there were so many persons who spoke to me about the fact that they did not have someone in the House representing them at that point so the House could hear what they felt about the bill, whether they were for or against it. There was a deep anger in people's hearts at the fact they had not had someone here to whom they could talk, to whom they could write or telephone. I see the hon. member from Sarnia has left. I know he tried to pinch-hit and take care of Sarnia, his ministry, and Ottawa-Carleton, but the people did not feel that he really belonged there, that it was just a draftee arrangement.
I think the people are intelligent. They are wise and they really want to participate. With the advent of TV in the House I find-I do not know whether other members are experiencing this-that I cannot move out of this Chamber without meeting people on the street, at meetings and events, who are saying, "We are delighted to have TV in the House; we feel more a part of the action and you are going to hear from us on certain aspects". I think TV is bringing this Chamber closer to the average person. You simply cannot go on with this poor show of putting over by-elections for longer periods of time. I think the people will rise up in anger. I just happen to think, Mr. Speaker, that my election and some of the majority I got was because the people were angry that they had been left one year without adequate representation.
I should like to move, Mr. Speaker:

Mr. Speaker, I feel like a jack-in-the-box, bobbing up and down, but as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections I am quite prepared to have the subject matter referred to the standing committee.
1 welcome, first of all, the opportunity to speak to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott), as well as to the bill of the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick). When the bill does get to committee I will not have the advantage of speaking to it, so I hope hon. members on the other side will allow me to agree with the sentiments expressed by my colleague, the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson).

speechtext: Don't talk it out.

subtopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AND CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO SHORTEN PERIOD WITHIN WHICH BY-ELECTIONS MUST BE CALLED
speechtext:
That is not my intention, though the best way to have a member talk a bill out is to interrupt him continually so that he has to extend his remarks. I think the hon. member should be commended, though I do have some reservations. I have reservations along the line of those expressed by the hon. member for Trinity. But notwithstanding those reservations, I am prepared to see the subject matter referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
There is an inflexibility in the period proposed by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton in Bill C-211. It provides for a period of 120 days for the calling of a by-election. Notwithstanding his arguments concerning other countries such as Australia, Canada has some particular weather conditions and physical features which make it difficult to hold by-elections within set periods of time.
The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith), who has one of the larger ridings, will agree with me that time is needed, especially in large constituencies, not only to organize the mechanics of the election but for the parties to select the proper candidates. In far flung ridings and those without principal centres, perhaps it would be difficult for parties to arrive at selecting an appropriate candidate within a period of four months.
I am not sure whether this particular comment is in order, but I would prefer to see the setting of elections to coincide with the summer. I am not sure how this would fit into our traditional British parliamentary system where there are minority governments. When I was elected, the election was as a result of the defeat of the government in the House. It occurred in May, but it could have occurred at any time during the year. Of course the New Democratic Party wanted to support the government at the time and prevented an election in the winter months.
When I was campaign manager for the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) there was the fall election of 1972. I received lots of complaints during that election campaign indicating that October was an inappropriate time to conduct
By-Elections
an election. This was in a constituency in metropolitan Toronto where people are close together and communications are good. In the fall many activities start, such as meetings of social groups, community affairs organizations and so on. The nights draw in, and the weather gets colder. Of course the weather does not get as cold in metropolitan Toronto as it does in Churchill; but older people are less likely to go out and vote on cold, dark, sombre days. I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would agree with this.
The timing of an election could deny the benefits of a democratic election to all elements in society. One advantage of the present system, which allows the government to call by-elections in a group, is that it affords the government and the opposition parties an opportunity to sound out public opinion in a number of constituencies. The by-elections this year were helpful to the government, because we happened to win five out of six by-elections. I am sure it was helpful to the official opposition to know their candidates were severely rejected in those by-elections, because that party had not felt the pulse of public opinion. As a result of those by-elections, I am sure the official opposition has taken into account the feeling of the electors as expressed in those results. Perhaps that caused the Conservatives to amend some of their party policies. It is not a bad idea to allow clusters of by-elections or mini-campaigns. There is a lot to be said for this kind of campaigning.
The hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton and the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton referred to the problems constituents have in not being served. This was a legitimate argument. It is unacceptable that ridings go for long periods of time without representatives. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned a lenghty spell in the parliament of 1940 to 1945. If it continues for more than a year, as was the case with St. John's West, it is unacceptable; although there were good reasons for that particular aberration in the case of St. John's West.
One of the largest ridings in Canada, that of the former hon. member for York-Scarborough, is in the position of having no representative at the present time. Mr. Stanbury had control over his resignation. Perhaps he expected a fall election and that there would be no vacancy. But of course there was no election. He had an opportunity in private life, which he felt he must take, and therefore he left. Likely there is to be an election in 1978. To call an election for York-Scarborough, a riding which will disappear after redistribution, because it is being divided up into five or six other ridings, would be a waste of taxpayers' money.
Before Mr. Stanbury resigned he made arrangements with the surrounding Liberal members-the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell), the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin), myself, and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson)-to help in any emergency. Of course we cannot provide the same quality of representation he provided, because we have our own large ridings, but any person in the present York-Scarborough riding can call up one of these other members. This was mentioned by Mr. Stanbury

November 25, 1977
By-Elections
in his final newsletter to his constituents. In fact tomorrow morning in my constituency office I will deal with two cases that have been referred to me from that riding. Perhaps that is possible in large metropolitan areas where there are numbers of constituencies, but in the rural areas that is not the case. Therefore I would accept the arguments made by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton.
Another question concerns cost. The hon. member for Trinity mentioned that it is expensive to conduct by-election campaigns continually, especially in the case of York-Scarborough.
This bill was introduced a year ago, but it never got to committee. This is the first time it has been read. It is unfortunate the Chief Electoral Officer did not bring in amendments, or perhaps attempt to talk about the subject matter of some of the amendments before committee at the moment in Bill C-5.
I am not sure whether I should be talking about the costs of running an election. The hon. member for Trinity mentioned that it is quite expensive to run elections in Canada. I should like to remind hon. members that it is very expensive for parties to conduct elections, whether they be by-elections or general elections. The expenditure allotment is inadequate. I hope the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton will address himself to that particular issue when debating the bill now before committee.
1 believe that with the increase in postal rates in the last two or three years-I think it will be 6 cents by April 14-it is quite obvious that while the reimbursement from the government will be increased, the expenditure limit will be held. I am not sure how members of the Conservative party feel. I know the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) feels quite strongly, as do other members of his party, that there should be some increase in the expenditure limit for elections. I just wanted to mention a point by way of concluding my remarks on this bill, that there will be some agreement in the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections that there be some increase in the expenditure limit, although perhaps not that expressed by the government in Bill C-5.
I would like to say in conclusion, because I do not wish to be the one who holds this bill up-I would send the bill to committee-that I support the principle, the thrust, the sentiments behind the bill, but the provision about the 120 days concerns me and I do not think all the questions have been answered. Nevertheless, the committee is probably the proper place for discussing all those reservations.
